‘Multiple people’ shot at fitness center in Washington
item.description:
Police were responding to a shooting in downtown Washington on Thursday as a local official said “multiple people” were shot at a fitness center.
The Washington police department said on X that its emergency response team was on the scene of an “active shooting” in the upscale Logan Circle area of the nation’s capital.
Police later said that the incident had resulted in a “barricade situation” and urged residents to avoid the area, which is about a mile north of the White House.
Brooke Pinto, a member of the DC City Council, said the shooting, which took place during the busy morning rush hour and sparked a massive police response, occurred at and outside a fitness center and “multiple people” had been shot.
The Washington Post quoted police as saying that at least five people had been injured.
Multiple law enforcement agencies could be seen at the scene of the shooting and police helicopters were hovering over the area.
Some residents were being evacuated from the area by police while others were being urged to shelter in place.
The Washington Sun quoted a member of the VIDA Fitness gym as saying that he was on a treadmill at the workout facility when the shooting began.
Michael Carney said he heard a “pop” and then saw someone on the gym floor who had been shot in the head.
“Everyone was kind of just hiding behind planters and stuff,” Carney told The Sun.

item.title: Eight Chinese students leave DU early after series of crude bomb blasts
item.description:
Eight Chinese students are leaving Dhaka University (DU) ahead of schedule following a series of crude bomb explosions on campus that raised security concerns.
Two have already returned to China, while the remaining six are scheduled to leave on Friday.
The students had come to DU to attend a special course on the Bangla language and Bangladeshi culture offered by the university's Institute of Modern Languages (IML). They were originally scheduled to complete their course and examinations and return home in late November.
Professor Dr MA Kawser, provost of Sir P J Hartog International Hall, the university's residential hall for foreign students, confirmed the matter to Dhaka Tribune on Thursday.
He said the eight students from China's Guangdong University of Foreign Studies became concerned after a series of crude bomb explosions on campus. Their families were also worried, prompting them to decide to return home early on the advice of their university.
The students were initially scheduled to return after completing their examinations in the last week of November. However, two have already left, while the remaining six have confirmed their flight tickets, Professor Kawser said.
He recalled that two of the students were passing near one of the explosion sites when a crude bomb went off. Witnessing the incident left them frightened and prompted their decision to return to China.
He added that the students would complete their remaining examinations through their university after returning to China.
Meanwhile, the hall authorities discussed campus security with other foreign students on Wednesday afternoon. They were assured that measures were being taken to strengthen security at the hall and across the university. The other students are currently monitoring the situation.
The IML offers special Bangla language courses for foreign students, providing an opportunity to learn about the language and culture of Bangladesh.
According to institute data, 15 students from two Chinese universities participated in the program in 2024, 19 from three universities in 2025 and 26 from four universities in 2026. Students from Guangdong University of Foreign Studies are among the participants.
A series of crude bomb explosions has rocked different parts of the DU campus over the past few days.
At least eight crude bombs exploded at six locations on Sunday evening.
Another explosion occurred in the TSC area on Monday.
Although no one was injured in those incidents, the explosions sparked panic across the campus.
On Tuesday, another crude bomb exploded in front of the academic building of the Faculty of Business Studies, injuring one person.
A separate explosion was also reported in the Shadow area beside the Faculty of Arts building on the same day.

item.title: Drug kingpins evade repeated raids at Feni’s Bede settlement
item.description:
Despite repeated anti-drug raids at Feni’s Lalpol Bede settlement, the alleged masterminds behind the drug trade remain at large, raising questions about the effectiveness of law enforcement operations.
In the latest raid on Wednesday, law enforcement agencies detained 14 people and seized Tk17.51 lakh in cash, a money-counting machine, 600 Yaba pills and 30 litres of locally distilled liquor, reports Bangla Tribune.
The three-hour operation, conducted from 5pm to 8pm, was led by Additional Superintendent of Police (Sadar Circle) Nishat Tabassum, with officials from the district administration and Feni Model Police Station.
Police said cases were being prepared against the detainees before they were sent to court.
Nishat said drug trading in the Lalpol settlement was widely known and police regularly conducted operations there. However, the alleged operators managed to escape by receiving advance information about the raids, she said.
She identified three people—Sohel, Tarek and Shirin—as the alleged controllers of the drug business, adding that they faced multiple cases.
The failure to apprehend the alleged ringleaders has raised concerns about whether repeated raids are disrupting the drug network or merely detaining people at the lower levels.
On plans to evict the settlement, Nishat said a committee had been formed through the district law and order committee to oversee the process. As many people live there, the eviction could not be completed in a single day, but preparations were underway to begin it soon.
She added that police operations would continue until the eviction was carried out.

item.title: PM leaves Antalya for Dhaka after attending COP31
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman left Antalya, Türkiye, for Dhaka on Thursday afternoon after attending the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) and the Antalya Leaders' Summit.
He departed Antalya Airport at 4:15pm local time by a Turkish Airlines flight for Istanbul, said PM's Deputy Press Secretary Hasan Shiplu.
Ambassador Subutay Yuksel, a high-ranking official at the Türkiye's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, saw the prime minister off at the airport.
Tarique is scheduled to leave Istanbul for Dhaka at 7:30pm local time and arrive at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka at 5:50am on Friday.
The prime minister arrived in Antalya on Tuesday on a three-day official visit to attend COP31 and the Antalya Leaders' Summit.
On Thursday, he addressed the High-Level Segment of COP31, outlining five urgent actions to address the needs of climate-vulnerable countries.
On the sidelines of the conference, Tarique held bilateral meetings with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Chinese Vice-President Han Zheng and Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev.
During the meetings, they discussed ways to strengthen bilateral ties, expand trade and investment, and enhance cooperation in addressing the impacts of climate change.
The prime minister also held courtesy meetings and exchanged greetings with several other world leaders and heads of international organisations during the conference.
Tarique and his wife Dr Zubaida Rahman attended a dinner hosted by Turkish President Erdoğan and First Lady Emine Erdoğan in honour of world leaders attending COP31.
Apart from participating in various programmes of the conference, he visited the Bangladesh Pavilion and an exhibition of environment-friendly jute products set up in the Green Zone.

item.title: Hailstorm, heavy rain damage paddy, potato fields in Rangpur
item.description:
A sudden hailstorm accompanied by torrential rain has damaged hundreds of hectares of ripe Aman paddy and early-season potato fields in Rangpur, leaving farmers fearing heavy losses.
The downpour continued for nearly two hours on Wednesday night, inundating farmland in Mithapukur and Pirgachha upazilas. Harvested paddy left in the fields has also been submerged, raising fears of rotting if water cannot be drained quickly.
At Baladipukur village in Mithapukur, vast stretches of farmland remained under one to one-and-a-half feet of water yesterday.
Farmer Solaiman said he had cultivated Aman on four bighas and harvested the crop four days earlier. However, the harvested paddy remained stranded in the field after the downpour.
Hailstorm, heavy rain damage paddy, potato fields in Rangpur. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
He has hired a shallow machine to drain the water, fearing the paddy will rot if it remains submerged.
Janab Ali Mondal, a farmer from Bairagiganj, said he had cultivated Aman on nine bighas. He had harvested paddy from two bighas, while hailstorms had knocked grains off the stalks in the remaining seven bighas, which were still partly unripe.
Similar damage has been reported in Anandnagar, Deuti and Parul areas of Pirgachha. Early-season potato fields in Damdama, Bairagiganj and surrounding areas of Mithapukur have also been inundated.
Farmers are trying to drain the water using shallow machines and have called for an immediate assessment of the damage and government assistance.
Saiful Alam, acting deputy director of the Department of Agricultural Extension in Rangpur, acknowledged the heavy rainfall and hailstorm. He said he had received reports of damage to paddy and early-season potato fields in parts of Pirgachha but was not yet aware of the extent of damage in Mithapukur.
He said field-level agricultural officials were advising farmers on ways to minimise losses.
According to the department, Aman was cultivated on 166,950 hectares in Rangpur this season, with a production target of 548,000 tonnes of rice. Early-season potato cultivation was targeted at 3,450 hectares.

item.title: Bicycles ease girls’ access to education in Panchagarh
item.description:
A group of teenage girls ride their bicycles in a line along rural roads, passing green paddy fields on their way to school, college or madrasa. Some wear white hijabs, while others sport colourful scarves, all dressed in blue uniforms.
The sight has become increasingly common in the remote villages of Atwari upazila in Panchagarh.
Until a few years ago, many girls in the area had to walk long distances to reach their educational institutions. The time and effort involved, coupled with limited transport options, often made it difficult for them to continue their studies. Bicycles are now helping change that situation.
With support from their families, many girls are learning to ride bicycles from an early age. By their teenage years, cycling has become an essential part of their daily lives.
Every morning and afternoon, groups of girls can be seen cycling along village roads. Besides travelling to school, they use their bicycles to attend private tuition, visit classmates and meet other daily needs.
Samsun Nahar, a Class X student at Dangirhat Adarsha High School, said cycling had made her journey to school much easier.
“Earlier, I had to walk a long way to school. It took a lot of time and left me tired before classes began. Now I can reach school much faster by bicycle. Riding with friends is enjoyable and makes me feel safer,” she said.
Saving time and gaining greater freedom of movement are among the main benefits of cycling. Journeys that once required lengthy walks can now be completed much faster, making it easier for girls to attend educational institutions farther from home.
Cycling in groups also gives girls a greater sense of security and confidence. Travelling together helps them feel less vulnerable to uncomfortable situations and potential harassment along the way.
Imdadul Haque, a parent from Sardarpara village, said distance and safety had previously been major concerns for families.
“We used to worry about how our daughters would get to school, particularly because of the distance. Now they ride together in groups. It saves time and has eased some of our concerns. Most importantly, they can continue their education,” he said.
Riding along village roads, from unpaved stretches to highways, is also helping girls develop mobility skills, confidence and a sense of independence.
The change has been driven largely by growing awareness and support among families. Many parents now encourage their daughters to learn to ride bicycles from an early age to help them continue their education. For families living far from schools and colleges, bicycles have become a practical and affordable means of transport.
Sharmin Parvin, headteacher of Atwari Government Pilot Girls' High School, said transportation played an important role in ensuring students' regular attendance.
“Travelling to educational institutions can be difficult for girls from remote areas, particularly when they have to cover long distances. Bicycles have eased that problem considerably. They are also helping girls become more confident and independent,” she said.
The benefits of cycling extend beyond making daily journeys to educational institutions easier. Improved access to schools and colleges can remove one of the practical barriers that often disrupt girls' education.
It can also contribute to efforts to prevent child marriage by helping girls stay in education, broaden their future opportunities and develop greater independence.
Jahidul Islam, acting upazila secondary education officer in Atwari, said access to transportation was important for expanding girls' education in rural areas.
“Bicycles are enabling many students from remote villages to travel to educational institutions more easily. This can help ensure regular attendance, maintain continuity in education and build confidence and independence among girls. Families and communities should encourage such initiatives,” he said.
The sight of girls cycling through Atwari represents more than just a convenient way of getting to school. It reflects changing family attitudes, progress in rural girls' education and the growing independence of young women.
As they pedal past green fields and along village roads, the girls of Panchagarh are moving towards a future where distance no longer has to stand in the way of education.

item.title: Two phones seized as SP accused of information leak
item.description:
A superintendent of police (SP) serving at the Chittagong Range Reserve Force (RRF) has been placed under surveillance over allegations of sharing sensitive police information with the activities-banned Awami League.
Police have seized SP Mohammad Jahangir Alam's personal and official mobile phones as part of an investigation into the allegations, said Chittagong Range Deputy Inspector General (DIG) Abdul Quddus Chowdhury.
He said Jahangir was called in to explain certain administrative matters before his two phones were seized. An investigation committee, headed by Additional DIG (Operations) Shafizul Islam, has been formed to examine the allegations.
The DIG said Jahangir had not been arrested, dismissing reports of his detention that had circulated among police personnel.
Additional DIG Shafizul Islam said Jahangir was summoned on Tuesday, but the meeting should not be described as an interrogation or detention.
The seized phones have been sent to the Special Branch in Dhaka for forensic examination. If the allegations are substantiated, the committee will submit a report to police headquarters, which will decide on further action, he added.
Sources at the Chittagong Range office said Jahangir, a 28th batch Bangladesh Civil Service (Police) officer, was accused of supplying internal and sensitive police information to the Awami League. They claimed preliminary evidence of information leaks had been found.
A senior police official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said information about Jahangir's alleged links with the activities-banned party had prompted senior officials to summon him. He was later released and is currently performing his duties, although he remains under surveillance.
Jahangir joined the police force on December 1, 2010, and is currently serving as deputy commandant of the RRF in Chittagong.
During the anti-discrimination student movement, he was posted as additional superintendent of police in Feni. He had also faced allegations of maintaining contact with leaders and activists of the activities-banned organisation during that period.

item.title: 10 police, 18 militants killed in Pakistan’s northwest
item.description:
Gunmen attacked police during an operation against illegal gold mining in northwestern Pakistan on Wednesday, killing 10 officers, while 18 militants died in the ensuing fighting, an official police statement said.
A statement by provincial police in Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa said officers were returning from a mine in the Gumbat area of Kohat district when militants opened fire on them.
In addition to the 10 police and 18 militant deaths, 12 police personnel were wounded, the statement said.
In the aftermath of the clashes, the Pakistani Taliban, the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), claimed responsibility for a series of attacks across the country, including one on a police convoy in the Gumbat area.
Earlier, a senior administrative official in Kohat told AFP that militants set two police vehicles on fire during the assault, while two other police vehicles and one private vehicle were missing.
Another senior administrative official in the Orakzai area of Kohat said that 10 militants belonging to the TTP were killed during a separate operation in the district.
A large quantity of weapons was also recovered from the militants, the official added.
Security forces are battling an intensifying militancy in the border province they say emanates from Afghanistan, an accusation its Taliban government denies.
A spokesman for a local emergency service earlier on Wednesday said there had been a “firing incident involving police personnel” in Kohat district, adding that rescue workers were treating a dozen wounded officers.
Relations between Pakistan and Afghanistan have been fraught since the Taliban authorities took power in 2021, and worsened after deadly border clashes in October last year that led to near-total closure of the border.
Clashes subsided after mediation, but the conflict intensified again in February, with Pakistan declaring “an open war” on its neighbor.
In a statement, Pakistan’s President Asif Ali Zardari condemned the attack, expressed his sorrow over the deaths of the police and said “national determination to completely eradicate terrorism from the country is unwavering.”
Pakistan’s foreign minister Ishaq Dar said he was “deeply grieved by the loss of precious lives in a cowardly terrorist attack on our police personnel in Kohat.”
Islamabad accuses Kabul of allowing militants responsible for deadly attacks on Pakistani territory to operate from its soil. Afghanistan’s Taliban authorities have denied the allegations.
Hundreds of civilians have been killed in fighting between the two countries since October last year, according to figures from the United Nations’ mission in Afghanistan.
Earlier this month, militants in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa killed two police officers assigned to protect a polio vaccination team travelling near the Afghan border.
The province was placed under emergency rule last month in a move authorities said came in reaction to the failure by the provincial government to act against militancy.
The imposition of emergency measures sidelined the last remaining bastion of power for jailed former prime minister Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party.
The special constitutional measures also set off a province-wide crackdown on Khan’s supporters, with hundreds of detentions.

item.title: Two garment factories in Gazipur shut indefinitely amid labour unrest
item.description:
Authorities have indefinitely shut down two garment factories in Gazipur following allegations that workers refused to work despite reporting to their workplaces and vandalized factory premises amid demands for a minimum wage hike.
Workers arriving at the factories on Thursday morning found notices at the main gates announcing the closures.
The factories are MM Knitwear Ltd and Mamun Knitwear Ltd, both located in Konabari.
The management of both factories announced the closures effective Thursday.
According to a notice signed by the deputy manager of the administration and human resources department of MM Knitwear Ltd, workers stopped working after the lunch break on Tuesday (November 10), demanding an increase in the minimum wage.
Despite repeated requests, the workers remained inside the factory but refused to work without any reasonable cause, the notice said. It added that they later brought workers down from different production floors, vandalised factory property and left the premises.
The notice further stated that workers resumed their work stoppage on Wednesday morning, creating disorder inside the factory through intimidation and physical altercations.
Describing the workers' actions as an illegal strike, the notice said the management was compelled to suspend operations indefinitely from Thursday to protect factory property and ensure the safety of lives and assets amid continued labour unrest.
The closure was announced under Section 13(1) of the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006. The notice said the date for resuming operations would be communicated once conditions became favourable.
Attempts to contact officials at the two factories for comment were unsuccessful.
Gazipur Industrial Police Superintendent Mohammad Amzad Hossain said the factory authorities had declared an indefinite closure. Police have been deployed to maintain normalcy in the area.

item.title: President stresses healthcare sector reforms to bring services to people’s doorsteps
item.description:
President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir today stressed the need for a comprehensive overhaul of the country's healthcare system, alongside a change in the mindset of all concerned, to bring medical services to people's doorsteps.

"A major transformation and reorganisation of the country's healthcare services is crucial to bringing healthcare services to people's doorsteps," he said.

The President said this while inaugurating the 1st International Conference and Dental Expo-2026 (BPSCON 2026), organised by the Bangladesh Prosthodontic Society, this morning.

The President said, "The country's healthcare system has become so complicated that accessing medical services has become difficult for ordinary people. Besides, the cost of dental treatment is so high that ordinary people cannot afford it."

Referring to the limitations of healthcare services at government hospitals, the President said, "In most cases, government hospitals lack the necessary physicians and adequate medical facilities. At the upazila level, physicians are often hardly available. As a result, ordinary people are compelled to seek treatment from unqualified practitioners."

He urged the relevant authorities to appoint an adequate number of government physicians at health centres in remote and marginalised areas.

At the same time, emphasising the importance of young physicians providing healthcare services in rural areas, he said, "Many young physicians do not want to go to villages after completing their studies. However, ordinary people will not receive medical services unless physicians work in rural areas."

"Many physicians are unwilling to go to remote areas. Even those who go to remote sometimes, move elsewhere after a few days for further training or other assignments. This mindset needs to change," he said, urging young physicians to develop a mindset of serving people in rural and remote areas.

"The country's brightest students study medicine or medical science, and the government makes substantial investments in this sector. However, the benefits of these investments are not reaching ordinary people," he added.

The President also called upon the relevant authorities in the healthcare sector to act sincerely to prevent various forms of existing mismanagement, saying, "The situation could be changed very easily if people had love and a sense of responsibility towards others."

Calling for initiatives to keep professional organisations free from partisan politics, he said, "Political affiliations should not influence professional activities. If initiatives are taken in this regard, many of the problems would be reduced considerably."

"The tendency to change everything in an organisation whenever the government changes must also come to an end," he noted.

"The country's people want change, and everyone must work together to bring about this positive change. To this end, all must continue working from their respective positions to establish a universal and people-friendly healthcare system in the country," he added.

Thanking the organisers for arranging the international conference, he said the Bangladesh Prosthodontic Society would further strengthen its position at the international level and make significant contributions to supporting the country's dental surgeons and improving dental healthcare services.

On the occasion, the President also shared his personal experiences regarding his dental problems and treatment and expressed gratitude to the physicians who have been treating him.

Earlier, the President unveiled the souvenir of the organisation, which also presented him with a commemorative crest.

President of the Bangladesh Medical and Dental Council Prof. Mohammad Saiful Islam and Dean of the Faculty of Dentistry at Bangladesh Medical University Professor Shakhawat Hossain delivered speeches as special guests.

The programme was presided over by President of the Bangladesh Prosthodontic Society Professor Abu Tayeb Md. Ahsan Ullah, while Member Secretary of the organisation's convening committee Md. Alamgir Kabir delivered the welcome address.

The organisation's General Secretary Professor Md. Masudur Rahman also spoke on the occasion.

item.title: Global Microsoft outage: steps to fix not going 'as expected'
item.description:
MICROSOFT-OUTAGES/

Outlook, Teams, Word 365 and other Microsoft products down in 74 countries, including Bangladesh.

Microsoft said on Thursday that efforts to repair a major outage of Outlook were not going as expected and the firm was seeking alernative solutions as users around the world were left without its crucial services.

The hours-long disruption, which Microsoft attributed to "elevated load" on its infrastructure, has hit email as well as products such as Teams and the AI assistant Copilot.

The impact of the outage has been felt globally, with users ranging from companies to governments reporting that they were unable to communicate via Outlook.

"We've monitored the status of the changes applied to improve serviceability and confirmed they're not taking as expected," Microsoft said on X.

"We're identifying alternate workstreams that can be applied to increase capacity," the tech giant added, without saying when service was expected to be fully restored.

The disruption went global within an hour, knocking out Microsoft products in 74 countries and territories, outage tracker Downdetector reported.

A map posted by Downdetector on X showed the outage affected users across the Americas and parts of Europe, Asia and Africa.

One of the impacted countries was New Zealand, where the foreign ministry sent a notice saying its "ability to receive emails has been affected by the global Microsoft outage. This also impacts all New Zealand Embassies, Consulates and Representative Offices around the world."

Microsoft initially said it was investigating outage reports "in the Americas," but later confirmed that the issue apparently affected "Microsoft 365 service connectivity for users in any region."

Microsoft 365 is the company's cloud-based subscription service that includes popular applications such as Outlook and Teams.

"We've determined a portion of infrastructure is experiencing elevated load across multiple regions, which is likely contributing to the connectivity errors," the company wrote on X.

"We're aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact," it added.

Downdetector, which tracks online outages, showed a sharp decline around 0450 GMT in users reports of disruptions in Washington and Hong Kong.

Thousands of users also reported issues with Teams and Copilot, according to Downdetector.

As the outage dragged on for hours, Microsoft posted a series of updates on X, detailing continued but unsuccessful efforts to restore full service.

In one update shortly after 6 pm Eastern Time (2300 GMT), Microsoft said it was "observing limited recovery" as it sought to route user traffic away from affected servers.

"As capacity is restored, users may experience a gradual recovery as their clients reconnect," the company added.

item.title: Nusrat’s home fire: Heated exchanges in parliament over cause of blaze
item.description:
A heated debate and repeated uproar erupted in the national parliament over whether a fire at the ancestral home of reserved-seat member of parliament (MP) Nusrat Tabassum was accidental or deliberately set. On Thursday, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed had to suspend his speech for some time because of protests by the opposition.

A fire broke out at the ancestral home of Nusrat Tabassum, a National Citizen Party (NCP) leader, in Kushtia on Wednesday night. The following day, opposition Chief Whip Nahid Islam and Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed exchanged remarks on the incident twice in parliament. The home minister’s second statement triggered a brief uproar and tension in the House.

Nahid Islam claimed that four petrol bombs had been thrown at Nusrat’s home, setting it on fire. Citing a preliminary investigation report, Salahuddin Ahmed, meanwhile, said investigators suspected that no petrol bombs had been used. It was highly likely to be electrical short circuit due to old wiring. However, he added that the government would take action accordingly if further investigation found evidence of sabotage.

According to Thursday’s agenda, the question-and-answer session was scheduled to be the first item of business. However, at the start of the session, opposition Chief Whip Nahid Islam rose on a point of order and raised the issue of the fire at Nusrat Tabassum’s home.

NCP convener Nahid Islam said concerns were growing over the safety of MPs, leaders of the July mass uprising and activists involved in the anti-fascist movement. He said, “Will this government provide any kind of security? If it cannot, let us know.”

Nahid Islam said, “If we have no human rights and if this government remains more concerned about the human rights of our enemies, then we will have to find our own way.”

Saying that it was clear who the targets of the attacks were, he warned the government, “If we are the first targets, they (the BNP) will be the second target. If our families are attacked, their families will also be attacked by the fascist forces. They are that brutal.”

Nahid said four petrol bombs had been thrown at Nusrat’s home in Daulatpur, Kushtia, setting it on fire. He said it was clear who the main targets were in the anarchy and sabotage being unleashed across the country by the ousted fascist forces.

The home minister had said that every crude bomb explosion at Dhaka University could not be described as deterioration in law and order. Nahid asked whether the situation could be described as deterioration in law and order when the home of an MP was set on fire.

Will be doubtful of probe’s impartiality after home minister’s remarks: Nusrat Tabassum

Home minister’s response

The home minister was not in parliament when Nahid Islam was speaking. He arrived a short while later and addressed the matter. The home minister said an investigation has been ordered to determine whether the fire had broken out accidentally or had been deliberately set. The Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB), fire service, administration and police would conduct a joint investigation.

Citing the BGB’s preliminary report, the home minister said the evidence was being assessed in consultation with local residents and law enforcement agencies. No sound resembling a petrol bomb explosion had been reported. No traces of petrol bombs had been found on the walls of the house, and no witness provided any information about petrol bombs. Overall, he said, the current assessment was that petrol bombs had not been used there.

The home minister said that a preliminary examination of all the evidence, including photographs, audio recordings and videos, suggested that the old house had faulty electrical wiring. One photograph indicated that the incident could have been caused by an electrical short circuit. However, he stressed that this was only an assumption and that a full statement could be made after the investigation was finished.

The home minister said a fire had broken out at MP Nusrat Tabassum’s village home, a tin-roofed house semi-concrete house. Her parents lived in a three-storey house about 20 metres away. Referring to the incident, he said nobody lived in the house where the fire occurred. There were two goats and other belongings inside. A general diary (GD) had already been filed over the incident, and police were investigating in accordance with it.

I will keep doing my work walking through fire: Nusrat Tabassum

Home minister is absolving those responsible: Nahid

Some time after the home minister’s statement, Nahid Islam stood up again on a point of order after the question-and-answer session had ended. He said the home minister referred to several video clips and a range of information. However, had he watched the video circulating on social media and elsewhere, he would have clearly seen that the entire house burst into flames in an instant because something was thrown at it from outside.

Stressing that Nusrat’s home was not abandoned, Nahid said it was not a place where livestock were kept; people lived there. People were also present on the night of the incident. They could have been killed. Nahid claimed that Nusrat Tabassum had been receiving various threats over the phone for several days and had also filed a general diary (GD). Therefore, he said, these incidents were not isolated.

Commenting that supporters of fascist forces had been celebrating on social media following the fire, Nahid Islam said the Kushtia district Awami League accepted responsibility for the incident. However, he said, the home minister had come to parliament and absolved them of responsibility.

Nahid said he had expected the home minister to announce how many hours it would take to arrest those responsible. “But, unfortunately, he came here in complete denial mode and rejected the incident outright,” he said.

Those who think they can intimidate us will only end up disgracing themselves: MP Nusrat

Home minister’s response and uproar

Responding to Nahid’s remarks, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said, “I have made a statement backed by information. An unfortunate incident occurred last night. The honourable opposition chief whip said the fire was deliberately set. Does that mean the investigation is already over?” His remarks prompted uproar from opposition members.

Addressing the opposition, the home minister said, “I would appreciate it if you could please listen while I am speaking. If you wish to speak afterwards, you may do so with the Speaker’s permission.”

The home minister then once again outlined the details of the incident, saying the preliminary investigation had found no traces of petrol bombs. Opposition members again protested loudly. The home minister then said, “If you wish, I can stop speaking.” Several members of the ruling party also responded with counter-protests.

The deputy speaker urged the minister to continue speaking, but opposition members kept up the uproar. The deputy speaker tried to calm them down and drew the attention of the opposition chief whip. However, at one point, the home minister sat down because he was unable to continue speaking amid the noise.

At that point, several NCP members, including Abdul Hannan Masud and Mahmuda Alam Mitu, stood up and continued speaking without microphones. Deputy Speaker Kayser Kamal repeatedly asked Hannan Masud to sit down. He said, “The home minister was speaking. Under no circumstances should he be prevented from delivering his statement. Please sit down. You can speak again if necessary.”

Fire at NCP MP Nusrat’s family home in Kushtia; petrol bomb attack alleged

The home minister then resumed his speech. As he once again described the incident, he brought up the goats. He said, “Two goats were kept in this house. And the goats...” Opposition members immediately began shouting again.

Mentioning that he has instructed law enforcement agencies to investigate the matter the home minister said, “If petrol bombs were thrown anywhere, there would be traces. You are free to conduct an independent investigation. If the fire was caused in some other way, it can be established after the investigation.”

The home minister said an unfortunate incident had occurred and that if there has been any sabotage or deliberate arson, action would be taken accordingly. If the fire had broken out accidentally, that could be established after the investigation report was submitted, he said. He added that it was not appropriate to make statements blaming the government.

The home minister urged everyone to wait, saying the investigation was under way. “We do not want to blame anyone. If any act of sabotage took place here, or if supporters of fascism were involved in any way, that too will be uncovered. But I do not want to make sweeping accusations, as was the practice in the past, by saying that this person or that person were involved,” he said.

item.title: ‘No slacking off’, cabinet secretary tells secretaries
item.description:
Cabinet Secretary Nasimul Gani has instructed secretaries to speed up their work and avoid delays. He gave the directive at a meeting with the secretaries on Thursday.

Asked about the meeting, Nasimul Gani told Prothom Alo that secretaries had been asked to ensure their work was properly organised and completed efficiently. He said they had been instructed to carry out tasks accurately and swiftly. No slacking off.

There is a substantial budget allocation, so the work must be carried out properly in line with that allocation, he said.

The main point is that work must be expedited and completed meticulously, Nasimul Gani added.

At the previous secretaries’ meeting in September, secretaries were instructed to accelerate government activities and complete tasks quickly, fill vacant posts without delay and focus on solar power to address the ongoing electricity and energy crisis, among other issues.

The secretaries’ meeting is a high-level policy forum of the government, attended by secretaries of different ministries and divisions. It discusses key government decisions, policy implementation and administrative coordination.

item.title: From Kalabogi to COP31: The case for developed-nation responsibility
item.description:
CLIMATE-COP31/

The village of Kalabogi sits on the Shibsa River in the Dacope sub-district of Bangladesh's southwestern coastal Khulna region. It is effectively a natural experiment: a coastal community where the effects of a changing climate can be observed not in projections but in practice—where climate change is not a forecast or a distant projection, but a daily, lived reality.

Known as a "hanging" or "floating village," Kalabogi homes stand on thatched and bamboo structures that must be relocated several times a year due to regular river erosion driven by climate change.

During my recent visit to the village, I witnessed their plight firsthand, as climate change—coupled with saltwater intrusion, frequent cyclones, and shifting weather patterns—continues to reshape their lives.

In Kalabogi and many other severely climate-vulnerable areas across Bangladesh, South Asia, and beyond, the water does not wait for conference decisions. It comes. It takes the land. It forces families to move their bamboo and tin shacks again and again—sometimes several times a year. Climate-vulnerable people in Bangladesh and elsewhere in the region and beyond do not speak the language of carbon budgets and mitigation targets. They speak the language of erosion and other climate-induced calamities. They know the rivers that once gave them fish and passage now take their homes.

As delegates gather in Antalya for COP31, the central question is not whether climate change is real. It is who bears responsibility for fixing it. The answer is unambiguous: developed nations, whose historical emissions created this crisis, must take primary responsibility. Not as charity, but as justice

The science is not complicated. Countries like the United States and the wealthy nations of Europe grew rich by burning fossil fuels. They filled the atmosphere with greenhouse gases over centuries. Bangladesh, a country of over 170 million people, contributes less than 0.5 percent of global emissions. Yet it sits on the frontlines of sea-level rise, salinity intrusion and increasingly violent cyclones. The people of Kalabogi are not responsible for the crisis swallowing their village. They are victims of a problem created elsewhere.

When a farmer in Khulna loses his land to erosion, he is paying for the industrial revolutions of Manchester and Pittsburgh. When a mother in Dacope struggles to find safe drinking water because of salinity intrusion, she is bearing the cost of decades of emissions from factories and automobiles in countries she will never visit. This is not a matter of generosity. It is a matter of historical accountability.

The United States, which has again declined to attend the negotiations, cannot ignore its role as the world's largest historical emitter. China and other emerging economies have responsibilities too, but their obligations differ in scale and timing. They are still developing. They have a right to grow. But the first debt is owed by those who became rich first.

At COP31, delegates from developing nations are again urging wealthy countries to honour their financial commitments. Bangladesh's environment minister has made clear that poorer countries are paying the heaviest price for emissions largely generated by rich nations. The demand is not charity. It is justice. Developed countries promised to mobilise $300 billion a year by 2035 to help vulnerable nations adapt. But promises made at climate summits have a way of evaporating when the cameras leave.

Climate finance that flows into government ministries and large infrastructure projects may never reach a family in Kalabogi whose embankment has crumbled. Adaptation projects designed in capital cities may not reflect the reality of a village that must relocate every monsoon. The gap between pledge and delivery is not an accident of bureaucracy; it is a consequence of a system that treats climate finance as discretionary aid rather than an enforceable obligation.

The absence of direct victims from Kalabogi and other vulnerable parts of the world in the COP31 process is not an accident. It is a structural flaw. Official delegations include bureaucrats, ministers and negotiators. They include representatives from international organisations and NGOs. But the people who have lost their homes, their farmland and their children's futures are rarely given a seat at the table.

Their stories are reduced to anecdotes in side events—if they are mentioned at all. This matters because the solutions being discussed in Antalya will only work if they reach the people who need them most. Without the direct participation of affected communities, climate action becomes an abstraction. A negotiation conducted entirely in the language of percentages and timelines cannot capture what it means to lose a homestead to the river, to watch salt creep into the soil that once fed a family, to send children away because there is no longer land to inherit. Participation is not a courtesy; it is a condition of effective policy.

The question of responsibility extends beyond emissions to the broader structure of global inequality. Developed nations have not only contributed most to the problem—they have also shaped the global economic system that leaves countries like Bangladesh vulnerable. Trade rules, debt structures and intellectual property regimes often work against the interests of developing nations seeking to build climate resilience. When Bangladesh seeks to access green technology, it faces barriers created by wealthy nations protecting their industries.

When it seeks loans for adaptation, it faces interest rates that deepen its debt burden. The very countries that caused the climate crisis are profiting from the solutions to it. The World Bank's 2022 assessment warned that climate variability and extreme weather events could cost Bangladesh one-third of its agricultural GDP by 2050. Food security depends not only on restoring agricultural production but also on wages, functioning markets and whether families can afford to plant crops again. A new crop variety may be suitable for saline soil, but remain beyond the reach of a farmer who has exhausted his savings and cannot afford to risk another failed harvest. Technology transfer, in other words, means little if it arrives as a product to be purchased rather than a resource to be shared.

This is where developed nations must step up. They must provide grants, not loans. They must transfer technology, not hoard it. They must fund locally led adaptation, not impose top-down solutions. And they must commit to loss and damage support that reaches the most vulnerable, not just the most connected. Bangladesh should pursue stronger international commitments while also advancing specific, actionable funding proposals. Its National Adaptation Plan provides an important starting point. The task is to identify priorities that clearly demonstrate who is at risk, what interventions are needed, how much they will cost and how they will be maintained over time.

Dr Saimum Parvez, the Prime Minister's Special Assistant on Environment, Forest and Climate Change, has said Bangladesh wants to take a leadership role in advocating for the rights of climate-vulnerable nations worldwide. Speaking at COP31, he noted: "Bangladesh is not merely highlighting its own climate crisis; it wants to take a leadership role in advocating for the rights of climate-vulnerable nations worldwide." This leadership is welcome, but it cannot substitute for the action that wealthy nations must take.

The world must recognise that climate justice is not an abstract concept. It is about a mother in Kalabogi wondering where her children will sleep tonight after the river takes another piece of land

Bangladesh has shown remarkable resilience and innovation—its early warning systems, community-based disaster preparedness and adaptive agricultural practices are models for the world. But resilience has limits. The people of Kalabogi cannot adapt indefinitely to repeated losses. They need real support—not loans that deepen their debt, but grants that restore their lives.

COP31, like the summits before it, will likely end with declarations and commitments. But for the families of Kalabogi, what matters is not what is signed in Antalya but what reaches their crumbling embankments, their saline fields and their displaced homes. The world must recognise that climate justice is not an abstract concept. It is about a mother in Kalabogi wondering where her children will sleep tonight after the river takes another piece of land. It is about a farmer who cannot afford to plant crops because the salt has poisoned his soil. It is about a community that has contributed almost nothing to global emissions yet bears the heaviest burden of the climate crisis.

Developed nations bear a primary responsibility in this collective endeavor. They must ensure that climate finance is accessible, support locally led adaptation efforts, and deliver loss and damage assistance in a manner that reaches those most in need. Absent these commitments, our promises risk appearing hollow. A summit that does not heed the voices of those affected by climate change would be a summit that has fallen short before it has even begun.

* The writer is a senior journalist and columnist.

* The views expressed in this article are solely those of the author.

item.title: Vegetable prices decline, coarse rice sees price hike
item.description:
Cauliflower, cabbage, radish and other early winter vegetables have started arriving in markets across the capital. With supplies increasing, prices of these vegetables have begun to decline compared to previous weeks. Broiler chicken and egg prices have also dropped over the past two weeks.

Vendors said, winter has already set in several parts of the country. It may take another 15 to 20 days for the cold weather to set in Dhaka as well as across all areas.

Typically, when the winter season peaks, vegetable production and supply increase, bringing prices down. However, many farmers grow early-season vegetables in the hope of making higher profits. These vegetables are now hitting the markets.

According to data from the state-run Trading Corporation of Bangladesh (TCB), the price of coarse rice has increased by Tk 3 per kg over the past week to Tk 50–58. Sugar prices have also risen by Tk 2 per kg to Tk 110–115.

This was observed in Mohammadpur Krishi Market, Town Hall Market and Agargaon Taltala Market in the capital on Thursday, as well as conversations with buyers and sellers.

At Krishi Market on Thursday morning, the first person to speak to was Tajul Islam, an employee of a private company. His shopping bag contained a medium-sized cauliflower and half a kilogram of beans, which had cost him Tk 65. He bought the cauliflower for Tk 35 and the beans for Tk 30. Adding half a kilogram of radish and a bunch of red amaranth would bring the total cost to Tk 100.

The shop also had newly harvested local tomatoes and potatoes. But Tajul did not buy either. Asked why, he said, “New tomatoes cost Tk 140 per kg, while new potatoes are Tk 120 per kg. If I buy these, I won't have enough money for the rest of my shopping. I'll wait until prices come down in a few days.”

Vendors said supplies of winter vegetables, including beans, cauliflower, cabbage and radish, were increasing. As these are early-season vegetables, their prices are still somewhat high. Prices are expected to fall further as supplies grow.

Prices of several vegetables have already declined. For instance, a large cauliflower that sold for Tk 60–70 two weeks ago was priced at Tk 40–50 on Thursday. The price of new potatoes has also dropped by Tk 30 per kg to Tk 120. Old potatoes, however, are much cheaper, selling for Tk 20–25 per kg.

Green chilli prices have fallen by Tk 40 per kg to Tk 60–80. Locally grown tomatoes from the new season have also started arriving in the markets, selling for Tk 120–130 per kg. Imported tomatoes cost Tk 110–120 per kg. Prices of other vegetables have remained largely unchanged.

Broiler chicken, which had been selling for Tk 190–200 per kg for several months, has become cheaper by Tk 20 over the past two weeks, now costing Tk 170–180 per kg. The price of brown eggs from poultry farms has also dropped by Tk 10 per dozen to Tk 150.

item.title: A lifeline for cancer patients in Dhaka: Free stay, food, care and ambulance services
item.description:
At the age of two and a half, Shraddha Biswas was diagnosed with blood cancer. She is now five years old. Her parents, Rupa Rani and Bandhan Biswas, from Jashore, have been fighting a long and difficult battle to ensure treatment for their only child. It took considerable time to diagnose the disease, and the expenses were enormous. They came to Dhaka and began treatment at the National Institute of Cancer Research and Hospital in Mohakhali. They rented a house near the hospital at Tk 200 per day, in addition to the cost of food.

One day, Rupa Rani noticed an address on a piece of paper posted on a hospital wall. The address was ‘Mosabbir Memorial Alok Nibash’ in the Bashundhara Residential Area. 

Now, for the past two years, the parents have been staying at Alok Nibash whenever they come to Dhaka with their daughter for treatment. They do not have to pay anything for accommodation or meals. Nurses at the residence also monitor whether the child is taking her medication properly. The family receives counselling services as well. An ambulance service is available to transport patients between the residence and the National Cancer Institute. All these services are provided free of charge.

On the afternoon of 8 November, I spoke with Rupa Rani at the six-storey Alok Nibash. Shraddha was in a bit of a bad mood. She refused to leave her mother's lap and did not want to talk. Her mother had done her hair up with several clips.

Rupa Rani said that Shraddha's father works as a security guard at a private company, and the family lives in Jashore. There are hardly any facilities for treating childhood blood cancer there. A local doctor had initially told them that their daughter had thalassemia. However, after coming to Dhaka, they learned that she had cancer.

She said the cost of treatment was very high. Had they not found out about this residence, it would have been impossible for them to afford their daughter's treatment in Dhaka, along with accommodation and food expenses.

Even when her husband cannot come to Dhaka regularly, it does not create any difficulties. The residence takes care of all the necessary arrangements.

Rebekah Akhter, the residence’s patient coordinator, has been serving in this role since the beginning, in 2022. She said, “We have watched Shraddha grow up right before our eyes. However, many people who stayed here and received treatment at various hospitals have also passed away. It is heartbreaking whenever we think about them.”

Through a project called Alok Kantha, patients undergoing treatment and their family members receive training to make quilts, embroidered quilts (nakshi kantha), prayer mats, diary covers and other items during their free time

The residence is an initiative of the Bangladesh Cancer Aid Trust (BANCAT). Across its two facilities in the Bashundhara Residential Area, including another two-storey residence, a total of 85 cancer patients and their caregivers are receiving these services.

After finishing the conversation, Rupa sat her daughter beside her and began sewing a quilt.

Through a project called Alok Kantha, patients undergoing treatment and their family members receive training to make quilts, embroidered quilts (nakshi kantha), prayer mats, diary covers and other items during their free time. These products are sold at the Unimart supermarket chain.

The women who make these items receive a share of the earnings. They also have the opportunity to use the skills they acquire to earn a living and rebuild their lives after returning home.

The daily routine at the residence begins as early as 6 am Patients are taken by ambulance to the National Institute of Cancer Research and Hospital, Bangladesh Medical University, and Dhaka Medical College Hospital. Upon returning, they wash their hands and faces at the entrance, take the lift and head to their respective rooms.

Patients queue from midnight to get appointment for cancer treatment

The residence has separate floors for women, men and children. After entering their rooms and taking a bath, residents can head straight to the dining area, where staff members on duty serve them meals.

Lunch on 8 November consisted of pumpkin, chicken and lentils. In the afternoon, children were served milk and bananas in bowls.

A nutritionist visits twice a week to prepare meal plans and assess the overall quality of the food. Three meals a day are prepared for a total of 600 people across the two residences.

Abu Shahnaz Sanit works as an office staff member at Mosabbir Memorial Alok Nibash. He is from Cox’s Bazar and currently lives at the residence while studying in the first year of the Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) programme under the Bangladesh Open University.

A year and a half ago, his elder brother stayed at the residence while receiving cancer treatment. After his brother died at the age of 29, Abu Shahnaz began working there.

The story behind BANCAT

Nazmus Ahmed Albab, a garment factory owner and businessman, serves as the founder and executive director of BANCAT. Speaking to Prothom Alo, he said he was diagnosed with blood cancer in 2011, at the age of 45. He began treatment in Singapore within a week of his diagnosis and recovered within a year, returning to Bangladesh. However, his experience with cancer transformed him profoundly. He began wondering how people from poor backgrounds could afford cancer treatment.

He started visiting government hospitals and eventually wound up his business. He began raising funds and collecting donations for cancer patients. Initially, financial assistance was provided to cancer patients through the Bangladesh Cancer Aid Foundation.

In 2019, BANCAT was established, growing out of the foundation. People with family members affected by cancer, as well as others who shared the same vision, came together to support the initiative.

The organisation set out to build a compassionate support system to ensure dignity, empathy and essential assistance for cancer patients at every stage of their struggle. Since its establishment, BANCAT has directly and indirectly supported more than 2,500 people affected by cancer and their families.

More than 500 donors and partners—including individuals, organisations, and Bangladeshis living both in the country and abroad—have joined this humanitarian initiative. BANCAT currently has 15 trustees. Rokeya Afzal Rahman, an adviser to the former caretaker government, was its founding president.

Their parents said the children were getting nutritious meals and opportunities to play with other children. They said it would have been impossible to find such an environment anywhere else.

Nazmus Ahmed said that after returning to Bangladesh and visiting government hospitals, he realised that although cancer patients were receiving medical treatment, they were not getting the care and support they needed. He began thinking about how such support could be provided. This idea led to the launch of Alok Nibash in 2022, initially operating from a rented house in the Bashundhara Residential Area.

The residence is named in memory of Mosabbir

Colonel (Retd.) Modasser Hossain Khan, who was awarded the Bir Protik gallantry title for his role in the Liberation War, serves as BANCAT’s chief adviser.

Speaking to Prothom Alo, he said his son, Mosabbir Hossain Khan, died of brain cancer in 2002, at the age of just 17. His son received treatment in the United States.

In 2004, the Mosabbir Cancer Care Centre was established in Dhanmondi in his son's memory. After Alok Nibash began its operations, he got in touch with Nazmus Ahmed Albab.

Modasser Hossain Khan said, “I was also diagnosed with cancer. I am doing well now, although I am getting older. I asked Albab to bring Alok Nibash and my organisation together. The two organisations were merged under the name Mosabbir Alok Nibash.”

On 8 November, I spoke with several other residents at Mosabbir Alok Nibash.

Seventeen-year-old Abdul Hasib had to have his right leg amputated from the thigh. He now walks with the help of crutches. His father, Md. Milon, a daily wage labourer, travels with his son from Hatiya in Noakhali to Dhaka every 21 days for chemotherapy.

Previously, they used to stay in a rented house near the hospital in Mohakhali. To pay for his son's treatment, Milon had even mortgaged the small plot of land he owned.

Md. Jobel Mia, from Kulaura in Moulvibazar, works as a mason. His daughter, Takia Akter, is only two and a half years old. She was diagnosed with a rare form of cancer when she was 19 months old. She has completed 21 of the 31 chemotherapy sessions required at the National Institute of Cancer Research and Hospital.

About a month ago, Jobel Mia moved to the residence with his wife, Salma Begum, their daughter and their five-and-a-half-year-old son, Adil Hossain.

Many other residents also spoke about the relief the facility has brought them. As afternoon set in, the children at the residence began drawing, playing various games or enjoying the swings.

Their parents said the children were getting nutritious meals and opportunities to play with other children. They said it would have been impossible to find such an environment anywhere else.

A new dream: ‘Cancer Care Village’

Mahjabin Ferdous, a trustee and general secretary of BANCAT, has lost six members of her family to cancer, including her paternal and maternal grandparents, parents, paternal aunt and maternal aunt.

She said, “We are now dreaming of establishing a cancer care village called ‘Alok Bosoti’. Construction work has begun. Through our initiative, ‘One brick for Tk 1,000’, anyone can contribute to this project. The village will provide all services in one place through an integrated system. Work on the project has begun on five bighas of land in Singair, Manikganj.”

Nazmus Ahmed said he gave up his garment business after beginning his work with cancer patients and started collecting donations from people. As a result, members of his family began to think he had lost his mind.

In 2024, he was diagnosed with kidney cancer again and had to have one of his kidneys removed. However, he did not give up.

More than 200 people now make regular donations to support his initiative. Some send rice, others contribute lentils, while some sponsor individual beds. In this way, contributions from people make it possible to stand beside those affected by cancer and support them through their difficult journey.

item.title: BRTC’s electric buses will not hit Dhaka roads in January, tender revision delays project
item.description:
• The deadline for submitting bids under the initial tender was 4 November. At the request of contracting firms, it was extended to 8 November.

  • Pragoti and BMTF issued a re-tender on 10 November with revised conditions. The deadline for submission is 18 November.

An initiative to purchase 100 electric buses for the first time for the Bangladesh Road Transport Corporation (BRTC) fleet has been delayed.

The buses were supposed to be running on Dhaka’s streets by 15 January next year, but this will not be possible now. Sources concerned say the project has been delayed because amendments were made to the tender for purchasing the buses.

The contracting firms have raised suspicions over the tender amendments, suggesting that the conditions may have been changed to favour a particular company. BRTC, however, maintains that the changes were made to increase competition.

The BNP government has taken an initiative to purchase 200 electric buses. On 5 August, the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs decided to purchase the buses through the Direct Procurement Method (DPM), without inviting tenders.

In the first phase, 50 buses each will be purchased through Pragoti Industries Limited and Bangladesh Machine Tools Factory (BMTF). Another 100 buses will be procured in the second phase.

The estimated cost of each bus, including its charging station and infrastructure, is Tk 40 million (4 crore). The Ministry of Finance has approved a proposal to provide BRTC with a loan of Tk 8 billion (800 crore) at 1 per cent interest to purchase the 200 buses.

The buses were supposed to be running on Dhaka’s streets by 15 January next year, but this will not be possible now. Sources concerned say the project has been delayed because amendments were made to the tender for purchasing the buses.

Pragoti is the country’s only state-owned vehicle assembly company. However, the two companies will not manufacture the buses themselves; instead, they will bring them in from abroad through suppliers.

A BRTC source said the two companies had been assigned the responsibility to ensure the buses could be brought in quickly. They will select the suppliers through a tender and send their proposals to BRTC. The corporation will then place the proposals before the cabinet committee on government purchase.

According to the documents, the complication concerns an amendment to Clause 36 of the tender. The tender issued on 29 October required the manufacturer to have a collaborative relationship with a local representative or authorised distributor in Bangladesh.

The local representative was also required to have experience of supplying passenger or goods vehicles in Bangladesh during the five years immediately preceding the issuance of the tender.

On 8 November, BRTC Director Anupam Saha sent separate letters to the two companies, instructing them to amend the conditions. The letters called for experience in supplying ‘electrical equipment’ to be included alongside vehicle supply. They also required five years’ experience in supplying such equipment and providing related services.

Bus fares increased by 17 paisa per km

Conditions relaxed to increase competition

The deadline for submitting bids under the initial tender was 4 November. At the request of contracting firms, it was extended to 8 November. With the revised conditions, Pragoti and BMTF issued a re-tender on 10 November, setting 18 November as the new deadline.

Several contracting firms have questioned whether the addition of new conditions to the ongoing tender, requiring experience in supplying electrical equipment, is intended to favour a company with such experience.

BRTC Chairman and Additional Secretary Meer Ahmed Tariqul Omar told Prothom Alo that the government has relaxed the conditions to allow more companies to participate. He said both conditions should have been included in the original tender. The two officials responsible for the omission have been temporarily suspended, he added.

The two suspended officials are Abu Bakar Siddique, deputy general manager of the Planning Department, and Imam Hossain, a procurement officer. They were suspended on 8 November.

Questions have also been raised about whether they had attempted to commit irregularities by leaving out the conditions. When asked about this, Abu Bakar Siddique told Prothom Alo that amending tender conditions was the responsibility of the Procurement Department. He believes he has been suspended while action was being taken against the other official.

item.title: Former Nvidia CEO had a relationship with a second employee
item.description:
NVIDIA-CEO/

Ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an intimate relationship with a second employee, according to two people familiar with the matter, Reuters has learned.

The revelation follows two other extramarital affairs that led to his resignation Thursday. The two women are Alice Huang, who US intelligence suspects of being a Chinese spy, and Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care.

Reuters is not naming the second employee. Attempts to reach the woman were not successful.

Nvidia declined to comment. Powell, Jensen Huang and a representative for Nvidia's board did not reply to requests for comment. Alice Huang could not be reached for comment.

Jensen Huang admitted to an affair in a 8 November statement following the reports of his relationship with Alice Huang, without referring to her by name.

The former Nvidia CEO's decision to resign from the company could disrupt the AI industry that he helped shape. Nvidia has used its financial strength to help create an industry around AI through complex financial arrangements that ease the purchase of the company's chips. It has backed cloud computing companies and AI labs in order to do so.

Pressure on Jensen Huang, who is 63 and married, to resign mounted after reports of his affair with Alice Huang.

Nvidia's board appointed finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO while it conducts a search to replace Jensen Huang. The board is considering internal and external candidates for the job.

Earlier this month, Nvidia's board launched a probe, led by independent directors with outside legal counsel, into whether Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. It also expressed confidence in him at the time.

Shares fell 5.5 per cent on Thursday in active trading. The stock has shed more than 30 per cent of its value since its early October peak.

item.title: Students, rickshaw pullers, tea sellers masons and others can get Tk 10 lakh loan
item.description:
Looking to start a business but lacking capital? Securing a bank loan typically requires collateral. Also, small entrepreneurs and low-income professionals often fail to qualify because they lack the necessary documents and financial capacity.

Bangladesh Bank has set up a Tk 15 billion refinancing fund to bring small entrepreneurs, low-income professionals and other marginalised groups without collateral or adequate financial documents under the formal banking system.

Under the scheme, banks will receive refinancing facilities from the central bank at an annual interest rate of 1 per cent and lend to customers at a maximum rate of 7 per cent.

Individuals can borrow up to Tk 10 lakh, while group loans can go up to Tk 40 lakh. No collateral will be required for loans of up to Tk 5 lakh. The loan tenure will be five years.

The Financial Inclusion Department of Bangladesh Bank issued a circular on Thursday outlining the scheme.

According to the circular, farmers, small traders, low-income professionals, women entrepreneurs, students, members of expatriate families and people affected by disasters will receive priority. Persons with disabilities and members of the third gender will also be eligible. At least 25 per cent of the total loan disbursement under the fund must be allocated to women.

The directive, sent to the managing directors and chief executive officers of all scheduled banks, sets out the eligibility criteria, loan amounts, interest rates, collateral requirements and disbursement procedures.

Bangladesh Bank said the initiative aims to improve the living standards of marginalised and disadvantaged groups by involving them in income-generating activities and expanding financial inclusion. A new policy has been formulated for the scheme.

Who will be eligible for the loans

Priority will be given to micro and small entrepreneurs operating in neighbourhoods, local communities and villages. Eligible occupations include fishermen, cobblers, goldsmiths, hawkers, blacksmiths, potters, tailors, rickshaw and van drivers, carpenters, masons, painters and plumbers. People involved in repairing electrical and electronic appliances, making pickles and traditional cakes, as well as small-scale weavers and tea workers, will also be eligible.

Grocery and general store owners, mobile clothing vendors, mobile recharge and mobile financial service agents, information and internet service providers, street food vendors, tea and betel leaf sellers, book and newspaper vendors, flower, fruit and vegetable sellers, and people rearing poultry and livestock can also apply.

Beyond traditional businesses, the scheme will cover people involved in freelancing, nursery businesses, tree planting, embroidery, block printing and batik, cottage industries, handicrafts, food production and promising innovative ventures. Trained members of the Village Defence Party (VDP) will also be eligible for loans to undertake various income-generating activities.

Among farmers, marginal and landless farmers holding a Farmer Smart Card will receive priority. They must have a bank account opened with Tk 10. However, banks have been instructed to ensure that marginal and landless farmers without smart cards are not excluded from the scheme.

Small traders and low-income professionals affected by river erosion, tidal surges, cyclones, floods, drought, monga, fires, earthquakes, building collapses and pandemics such as Covid-19 will also receive priority. Low-income people living in coastal areas, chars and haor regions, as well as members of ethnic minority and disadvantaged communities, will be eligible.

Family members of expatriates who receive remittances, migrant workers who have returned from abroad and their family members will also receive priority. People with special needs, persons with disabilities and third-gender customers will be prioritised for loans to engage in any income-generating activity.

Loans for students

The scheme also includes special provisions for students. Underprivileged, insolvent, or dropout students up to the age of 25 who hold student banking accounts may receive loans for vocational, technical, information technology and other training programmes. In such cases, a guardian must provide a repayment guarantee.

Loans may also be provided to cover the costs of higher education, including MBBS, BDS and engineering studies, as well as the purchase of necessary educational materials. A guardian's repayment guarantee will also be required for these loans.

Individual loans up to Tk 10 lakh, group loans up to Tk 40 lakh

An individual customer or micro and small entrepreneur can borrow up to Tk 10 lakh. The maximum amount for a group loan is four times that amount, or Tk 40 lakh.

To get a group loan, two to five people must form a group. Each member can borrow up to Tk 8 lakh. All members will be individually and jointly liable to the bank for repayment.

Applicants must have a bank account with Tk 10, Tk 50 or Tk 100 as the opening deposit. Those without an account will have to open one. The approved loan amount will be deposited into that account.

According to the Bangladesh Bank directive, loans of up to Tk 5 lakh will not require collateral. For loans exceeding Tk 5 lakh, reasonable collateral may be required depending on the relationship between the bank and the customer.

For loans of Tk 25,000 or more, banks may, at their discretion, use the Bangladesh Bank Credit Guarantee Scheme. The guarantee fee must be paid by the bank from its own funds.

Interest rate capped at 7pc

Shariah-based banks will also be able to provide loans under the scheme. However, their annual profit rate cannot exceed 7 per cent.

According to the Bangladesh Bank directive, borrowers will have up to five years or 60 months to repay loans. A grace period of up to six months may be allowed during which instalment payments can be deferred.

Excluding the grace period, banks will have to repay the principal, interest or profit, and service charges to Bangladesh Bank in quarterly instalments. At the customer level, banks may set repayment schedules on a monthly, quarterly, half-yearly or annual basis.

Before approving a loan, banks must obtain the customer's Credit Information Bureau (CIB) report. However, no charge or fee can be collected from customers for obtaining a CIB report for loans or investments of up to Tk 3 lakh.

How to get the loans

Bangladesh Bank said banks can distribute loans under the scheme through their branches, sub-branches, agent banking outlets, mobile financial services, online banking and internet banking.

Banks may charge service fees approved by their boards for disbursing and collecting loans through agent banking or mobile financial services.

However, they cannot collect any additional processing fee from customers for loans or investments beyond the charges permitted under Bangladesh Bank's Schedule of Charges guidelines.

Banks will have to conduct regular monitoring to ensure proper loan disbursement, recovery and use of funds by customers. They must submit reports to Bangladesh Bank by the 15th of the month following each three-month period.
