Is our healthcare system built for a climate crisis?
item.description:
Every monsoon, Dhaka’s hospitals follow a mundane, predictable routine. The corridors at Mugda Medical College Hospital and Dhaka Medical College Hospital overflow with patients burning with high fevers, platelets dropping, and families frantically searching for intravenous fluids and blood donors.
Months later, when floodwaters recede from low-lying districts or a blistering April heatwave descends on the capital, the wards yet again get overcrowded, this time with patients suffering from waterborne illnesses, heatstroke, and acute kidney issues.
We treat each surge as an isolated seasonal emergency, still the common thread tying these crises together is no longer just a pathogen or a sluggish city corporation cleanup drive. It is a rapidly warming and increasingly volatile climate.
And right now, Bangladesh’s healthcare system is fighting a 21st-century climate war with 20th-century, reactive armor.
In real time, climate change is redrawing Bangladesh’s epidemiological map, and the data from our own health system leaves no room for denial.
According to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), dengue has shattered every historical boundary. After the catastrophic 2023 outbreak that saw 321,179 hospitalizations and 1,705 deaths, the crisis has refused to recede into a mere seasonal nuisance.
In 2025, DGHS recorded over 102,800 cases and 413 fatalities and by November 2026, nationwide hospitalizations have already surpassed 155,000, claiming 479 lives, with significant surges extending into post-monsoon autumn and spreading across all 64 districts.
The Aedes mosquito’s breeding cycle gets accelerated with warmer microclimates and erratic rainfall, turning a once-localized monsoon infection into a year-round national emergency.
Meanwhile, the crisis influences far beyond mosquitoes. Along our low-lying coastline in Khulna, Satkhira, and Bagerhat, rising sea levels and intensifying cyclones are driving severe salinity intrusion into freshwater aquifers.
Public health studies in coastal Bangladesh show that residents consuming moderately saline drinking water (above 2,000 mg/L) face a 42% higher risk of developing hypertension compared to those drinking fresh water.
In coastal subdistricts like Dacope, tubewell sodium levels routinely exceed the World Health Organization’s 200 mg/L threshold. It pushes the daily sodium intake from drinking water alone near the WHO’s entire daily limit of 2 grams and driving alarming spikes in gestational hypertension and pre-eclampsia among pregnant women.
Inland, extreme urban heatwaves are turning concrete-heavy cities into thermal traps, pushing emergency rooms past their limits with heat exhaustion and cardiovascular strain.
Our public health apparatus remains trapped in a cycle of crisis management, despite these unmistakable numbers. We wait till the hospital beds overflow, forcing facilities like Mugda Medical College Hospital to scramble to triple their dengue ward capacity mid-outbreak, before declaring an emergency.
Municipalities launch reactive mosquito-fogging campaigns only after community transmission has peaked. Relief teams distribute oral rehydration salts and water-purification tablets after floodwaters have already submerged community clinics and Upazila health complexes.
A reactive system is inherently expensive, tiring, and deadly. By the time an outbreak registers in traditional hospital admissions data, transmission is already out of control. Worse, extreme weather events frequently cripple the very facilities meant to save lives, flooding ground-floor pharmacies, knocking out power grids during severe heatwaves, and severing supply chains for essential medicines.
Building a climate-resilient health system
Transitioning from firefighting to foresight requires two structural shifts in how Bangladesh plans and finances public health:
This means elevating critical infrastructure such as generators, oxygen plants, and medical storage above projected flood levels, integrating solar microgrids to keep cooling systems and life-support running during grid failures, and installing dedicated rainwater harvesting and desalination units in salinity-affected zones, where rainwater has been shown to cut drinking-water sodium exposure by over 95% compared to tubewells.
If meteorological models forecast an unseasonably warm, wet spell, municipalities and hospitals can pre-position IV fluids and NS1 rapid diagnostic kits, deploy targeted larviciding, and alert communities weeks before the first wave of fever patients arrives at the emergency.
Climate change is not a distant environmental abstraction for Bangladesh, it is sitting in our hospital waiting rooms today. Treating every dengue surge, cholera outbreak, and salinity-linked stroke as an unexpected shock guarantees that our doctors will remain overwhelmed and our most vulnerable citizens will pay the price.
If we want a healthcare system capable of surviving the decades ahead, we must stop measuring its strength by how heroically it scrambles during a disaster and start measuring it by how effectively it prevents the crisis from reaching the hospital doors in the first place.
Ashiana Reaz works at Democracy International (DI) and writes on public policy, environmental, and public health issues.

item.title: A fight for our existence
item.description:
Last Friday, three of my colleagues visited Haji Mazar Basti in Tongi, on the outskirts of Dhaka, on a reporting assignment to expose an illicit drug trade that has operated there unabated for far too long. They had no idea that a sophisticated CCTV network run by the drug cartel was recording their entry into the slum alleys in real time. Inside, they found brisk, open trading in drugs of every kind in broad daylight, completely unchecked by the state’s law enforcement apparatus.
While investigating this open narcotics trade, the three-member team was ambushed by an armed gang of 20 to 25 people. The Dhaka Tribune journalists endured unimaginable torture at the hands of these drug ruffians, who held them captive for three hours, beat them, threatened their lives at gunpoint, and robbed them of their belongings.
Since that barbaric attack, very little has happened -- not that we expected much -- apart from our newspaper's truthful reporting on the trade, the filing of a police complaint, and strong assurances from senior police officials that raids would be conducted and legal action taken against the perpetrators.
Badly injured and mentally traumatized, the three victims are still undergoing medical treatment. One continues to suffer from lightheadedness and hearing impairment.
Local residents later told us that last Friday’s assault on the Dhaka Tribune team was one of the worst, though not the first, such incidents in Haji Mazar Basti. Recently, journalists from at least two other national dailies also fell victim to the same tyrants.
It is the very spot where retired serviceman KM Tahsif Sauri was last seen before his tragic death. Tahsif went missing after leaving his family’s residence in Uttara on the evening of October 27, 2026. The following afternoon, Tongi River Police recovered his body floating near Rajabari Ghat in the Turag River, identifying him through an iPhone and wristwatch found on his person.
I stand to be corrected, but to my knowledge, since the recovery of his body -- and the subsequent discovery of his motorbike near the slum -- there has been no official drive to dismantle this notorious drug den.
In writing this, I do not mean to suggest that our law enforcers never raid criminal hideouts. They do. And when they fail to act, we see episodes such as that involving former junior minister Ishraque Hossain, who recently took matters into his own hands to fight neighbourhood drug dealers -- an act that ultimately cost him his ministerial job.
No sane person would endorse a public official taking up arms to chase down drug dealers. Yet one can certainly empathize with his frustration after dozens of pleas at official coordination meetings went unheard and the police failed to meet basic public expectations.
The Ishraque episode is a telltale sign of how law enforcement agencies, and the higher-ups who direct them, have failed citizens who ask only that an elected government free their neighbourhoods from an ever-expanding drug network.
To be fair to our law enforcement agencies regarding Haji Mazar Basti, they have conducted special drives there in the recent past. In May this year, police arrested 38 people and uncovered a concealed, air-conditioned luxury drug den complete with an escape tunnel.
Two months later, police arrested 42 more suspects, seized heroin and yaba, and disconnected electricity and internet connections to roughly 300 rooms suspected of being used for drug trading. Then, in August, authorities conducted eviction drives, demolishing around 100 illegal structures used as drug dens.
This raises an obvious question: How does the gang keep returning to operate a sprawling narcotics business in the very same area, time and again?
To understand this, we must look at Bangladesh’s thriving political economy, where political patronage quickly comes to the aid of illicit operations whenever they face the wrath of law enforcement.
Allegations are rife that, regardless of who holds power in the central corridors of the state, narcotics dealers at strategic distribution points enjoy vital political protection from both sides of the political aisle. That protection gives them the audacity to intimidate, terrorize, and unleash violence against any journalist who dares to expose them.
Why, then, is the press so determined to expose the drug threat? The answer is simple: It is a fight for our very existence.
We are living dangerously in this country. If police records and media reports are any indication, scarcely a day goes by without news of drug addicts killing or injuring people -- most often family members who refuse to give them money for a fix or neighbours who try to stop them. If we collectively fail to halt the rapid spread of this thriving market, it will soon catch up with every one of us in one way or another.
I will refrain from naming the specific spots in Dhaka where drugs are readily available. All it takes to score is the urge for a kick, the cash to pay for it, and knowledge of the selling points.
The media today is awash with reports on these hotspots and their unchecked trade. Just the other day, I read about a Toyota Land Cruiser Prado carrying 300,000 yaba tablets that set out from Cox’s Bazar for Dhaka on August 17. After stopping in Chittagong for a day, the vehicle took the Dhaka-Chittagong highway before being intercepted by the district detective branch police in Comilla.
According to reports, nearly 2.7 million yaba tablets were seized in six major incidents along the Cox’s Bazar border in the preceding five months alone. Five of those consignments were destined for Dhaka, from where, according to investigation sources, the drugs were to be distributed nationwide. Law enforcement data show that the largest consignments entering through our borders are now routed through metropolitan areas before being distributed across the country.
At the same time, the country’s eight major cities -- Dhaka, Chittagong, Rajshahi, Gazipur, Rangpur, Khulna, Barisal, and Sylhet -- have emerged as massive drug markets in their own right, largely due to their dense populations.
Data from pending court cases reveal the scale of this urban spread. Official figures indicate that 47,948 serious drug cases, carrying minimum sentences of five years or more, are awaiting trial in these eight metropolitan areas, out of 166,333 such cases pending nationwide. Nearly 29% of Bangladesh’s most serious drug cases are concentrated in these eight cities.
Before drawing the urgent attention of those in high offices to this crisis, let us briefly review how Bangladesh reached a point where the drug menace has become so pervasive.
Recall 2018, when the then government embarked on a nationwide "war on drugs" -- around the same time that the controversial Digital Security Act was enforced despite fierce opposition from civil society, rights bodies, and journalists. Over the next two years, Bangladesh witnessed at least 500 to 1,000 deaths in controversial "crossfire" shootings.
Then, in 2020, the killing of a retired serviceman at the hands of rogue policemen -- allegedly on the payroll of narcotics traders -- sparked a nationwide outcry. It compelled the government to take a measure almost unheard of in contemporary world history: Withdrawing and replacing the entire police force of Cox’s Bazar district, comprising between 1,100 and 1,400 personnel.
Fast-forward to 2026. In August this year, our current home minister, who hails from Cox’s Bazar, acknowledged that yaba tablets entering across the border were being distributed nationwide, ruining a large section of our youth. He spoke of preparing an “impartial list” of top drug traffickers as part of the government’s effort to curb smuggling and strengthen narcotics control.
When we put all these developments together -- the widespread crossfire killings of the late 2010s, the withdrawal of an entire district’s police force, and the unabated narcotics trade stretching from Gendaria’s Ghuntighar (of Ishraque fame) to Tongi’s Haji Mazar Basti -- a clear pattern emerges.
It is a cycle of half-hearted administrative measures, repeated empty assurances, and a section of politicians profiting from the proceeds of a thriving illicit market. Slowly but surely, and perilously, this network is engulfing the country like a spiderweb.
Now, it is up to us to decide: Do we truly intend to free ourselves from the grip of this drug crisis, or will we allow it to destroy the future of our children and generations to come?
Reaz Ahmad is Editor, Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Jaiswal declines to comment on reports that Delhi wants Bangladesh to send military aircraft to bring Hasina back
item.description:
India’s Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal did not respond to a question about media reports that New Delhi wants Bangladesh to send a military aircraft to bring ousted former prime minister Sheikh Hasina back to the country.

A journalist raised the issue during a question-and-answer session at the Indian Ministry of External Affairs briefing in New Delhi on Friday.

The journalist said, “There are a few reports saying that New Delhi wants Bangladesh to send a military aircraft to bring (former) prime minister Sheikh Hasina back from New Delhi, and has also sought assurances that she will be given an opportunity to appeal her death sentence and face a fresh trial over the 2024 crackdown. Any confirmation or communication regarding that?”

The spokesperson did not answer the question. He said, “On the other question you had raised several scenarios, I have nothing to say on that.”

More questions concerning Sheikh Hasina were raised at the briefing. A journalist asked whether her possible return would be through a land port or by air. The journalist also wanted to know whether the Indian government had made any preparations for Hasina’s return or was concerned about the complicated issue. Jaiswal did not answer these questions or make any comment.

The Bangladesh government has been requesting India to extradite Sheikh Hasina under the extradition treaty between the two countries. Hasina has been sentenced to death in a crimes against humanity case over the killings during the July mass uprising. India has yet to respond to the request.

Meanwhile, Sheikh Hasina has announced that she wants to return to Bangladesh in December, at any cost. Reuters recently reported that Hasina had written to the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi seeking a passport and national identity card.

On Thursday, BBC Bangla published a report on Sheikh Hasina’s announcement that she would return to Bangladesh. The report suggested that Hasina had not announced her return without India’s consent. However, it mentioned two conditions set by India.

First, Sheikh Hasina had arrived in India aboard a military aircraft of the Bangladesh Army. If she is to be taken back, the Bangladesh Army will have to carry out that task as well. Her return could be by land or by air. The second condition was that Bangladesh would have to assure India that Hasina would have the opportunity to appeal her death sentence and that the trial over the July killings would begin afresh.

At Friday’s briefing, Jaiswal was asked about the reports and whether there was any truth to them. He was also asked whether the government would say that reports of such an initiative were untrue. In response, the spokesperson repeatedly said that he had nothing to say or comment on the matter.

In response to a question about Sheikh Hasina’s extradition, Jaiswal repeated his earlier position. He said, “Extradition is a legal matter and it will be dealt with accordingly.”

The briefing also addressed the postponement of the India-Bangladesh consular dialogue. Asked why the meeting, scheduled to be held in Dhaka on 17 and 18 November, had been postponed, Jaiswal said it would take place on a mutually convenient date.

Jaiswal further said that many reports had emerged following the postponement of the consular meeting. Several reports had also been published in India.

He said, “India desires a positive, constructive, and forward-looking relationship with Bangladesh. Accordingly, initiatives have been taken and meetings held under structured mechanisms in areas such as trade, railways, water resources, and border management, among others.”

Following up on his response, Jaiswal also said the two countries’ consular dialogue would also discuss matters relating to revised travel arrangements. The meeting would be held on a mutually convenient date. India remained ready to discuss all bilateral issues with Bangladesh through the existing mechanisms, including at the technical level. In short, the consular dialogue would take place on a date convenient to both countries.

item.title: Jail terms, fines proposed for creating content by harassing animals
item.description:
It is a sunny day. A fox is resting in the middle of a vast mustard field. Suddenly, two drones begin flying just a few feet above its head. The fox starts running in fear. In the pursuit of creating content for humans, its moment of rest turns into one of terror.

Another video shows a dog sleeping on the grass beside a road. A young man approaches and attaches several balloons to the dog's tail using clips. Later, the balloons are burst by throwing stones at them from a distance. The loud noise wakes the dog. In panic, the animal jumps up and runs frantically in different directions.

Many people are making videos by harassing animals in this way. They are circulating these videos on social media in the hope of increasing views. However, creating and publishing such content may now lead to imprisonment and fines.

The first video was published on a Facebook page named ‘Banglar Drone’ in May this year. The video, captioned ‘Sheyaler songe droner mojar lorai (A fun fight between a fox and a drone)’, has been viewed 781,000 times. The page has over 100 videos made by harassing foxes and their families.

Meanwhile, the video of the sleeping dog being harassed was published by a Facebook user. Their Facebook profile is full of various videos of disturbing dogs. The video in question has nearly 500,000 views. There are more than 100 such pages and profiles on Facebook.

The proposed amendments to the Animal Welfare Act have recommended bringing not only those who create and publish content by harassing animals but also those who assist in such activities under punishment.

The proposed amendments to the Animal Welfare Act have recommended bringing not only those who create and publish content by harassing animals but also those who assist in such activities under punishment.

Creating videos by disturbing sleeping, resting or mating animals and publishing them on social media may lead to up to six months in prison or a fine of Tk 50,000, or both.

This provision on punishment has been added to the proposed amendments to the Animal Welfare Act, 2019. Under the proposed provision, this will be a cognisable offence.

Causing fear among animals will also be an offence

The Animal Welfare Act, 2019, had 14 sub-sections under Section 6. The proposed amendment has added sub-section (ṇ). This sub-section includes creating and publishing content by harassing animals as an offence.

Not only harassment, but creating and publishing videos by frightening animals by placing a reflection in front of them or attaching an object to their bodies will also carry the same punishment. Assisting in the production of such content will also be considered an offence.

Department of Livestock Services Acting Director General Md Shahzaman Khan told Prothom Alo that the draft amendments to the law had been sent to the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock. It has currently been published on the ministry's website to seek opinions from stakeholders. After receiving feedback and making necessary additions and deletions, the draft will be sent to the Ministry of Law for vetting.

Shahzaman Khan said the initiative to amend the law had been taken to protect animals from various forms of cruelty and make the legislation relevant to the present time in line with the government's intentions.

7 types of offences to become cognisable, non-bailable

Under the Animal Welfare Act, 2019, offences involving cruelty to animals were non-cognisable and bailable. The proposed amendments recommend making offences under seven sub-sections cognisable and non-bailable.

Sub-section (ch) of Section 6 of the draft law states that releasing an animal into a populated area while it is sick or with the intention of killing it will be a cognisable and non-bailable offence. Similarly, using animals as bait, engaging them in fights or inciting them to fight will also be considered offences under sub-section (chh).

Sub-section (nio) of the same section states that the same provision will apply to using animals as targets in shooting or archery competitions or releasing them to be pierced by bullets or arrows.

Under sub-section (ta) of Section 6, it has also been proposed that selling an animal suffering from pain due to hunger, thirst or other forms of cruelty without providing treatment will bring the offender under the same punishment.

Besides, the draft amendments propose making the killing of ownerless animals under sub-section (2) of Section 7, and removing sensitive tissues from an animal's body, cutting off its organs or altering its physical structure under sub-section 1 of Section 10, cognisable and non-bailable offences. Attempting or assisting in such acts will also be considered offences.

Knowingly feeding animals medicines, food or poisonous food that is harmful to them, or administering poison that causes their death, permanent organ damage or loss of normal functional ability, will be a cognisable and non-bailable offence under sub-section 1 of Section 11.

However, this provision will not apply when an animal is anaesthetised or given a painless death for legitimate reasons, following the written advice of a veterinary surgeon and the prescribed procedures.

Fines and prison terms increased

Under the Animal Welfare Act, 2019, several offences carried a provision of six months' imprisonment or a maximum fine of Tk 10,000, or both. These include failing to provide animals with necessary food or force-feeding them excessively, killing ownerless animals and using animals declared physically unfit to carry loads.

Although the proposed amendments have kept the prison term unchanged at six months for these offences, they recommend increasing the fine to Tk 200,000.

Under the previous law, removing sensitive tissues from an animal's body, cutting off its organs or altering its physical structure with the intention of causing harm carried a maximum prison term of two years or a fine of Tk 50,000, or both. The new draft proposes increasing the prison term to three years and the fine to Tk 500,000.

There are also provisions to increase the punishment if an animal dies or suffers organ damage due to the administration of poisonous food or medicine. The previous law prescribed a maximum of two years' imprisonment or a fine of Tk 50,000 for this offence. The proposed amendments seek to increase the punishment to three years' imprisonment or a fine of Tk 500,000, or both.

There are also provisions to increase the punishment for using animals as bait, shooting or piercing them with arrows, and selling sick animals without treatment despite their suffering from hunger, thirst or cruelty. These offences may carry a maximum of three years' imprisonment or a fine of Tk 500,000, or both.

Concerns over killing and removal of stray animals

Animal rights activists have welcomed the initiative to amend the Animal Welfare Act. However, they have also expressed concerns over the possible misuse of some provisions in the draft.

Rakibul Haque Emil, founder and chairman of People for Animal Welfare, told Prothom Alo that the Animal Welfare Act, 2019, had failed to play an effective role in ensuring the welfare of animals in the country. The current government has taken the initiative to amend the law. The proposals to make certain offences cognisable and non-bailable and increase the severity of punishments are encouraging.

However, referring to the provision allowing the killing and removal of animals under sub-section 1 of Section 7 of the proposed law, he said there were concerns over the possible misuse of this provision.

Rakibul Haque said incidents of killing and removing animals occurred more frequently in the case of stray dogs. The issue should be considered seriously before the law is finalised.

item.title: No possibility of fire at Nusrat’s house from short circuit: Rural electricity official
item.description:
An electrical short circuit could not have caused the fire at the ancestral home of Nusrat Tabassum, joint convener of the National Citizen Party (NCP) and a member of parliament from a reserved women’s seat, said Tozammel Haque, assistant general manager (operations and maintenance) of the Pragpur Rural Electricity Sub-Zonal Office in Kushtia.

Following the fire at Nusrat’s ancestral home late on Wednesday night, officials of the local rural electricity office removed the electricity meter. The operation was overseen by Tozammel Haque, AGM of the Pragpur Rural Electricity Sub-Zonal Office.

The rural electricity official inspected the burnt house again today, Friday. Asked about the incident, Tozammel Haque told Prothom Alo that he had inspected the meter, the wiring and the main switch connected to the meter at the scene.

He said the cut-out was found intact upon inspection. The transformer fuse had not blown either, nor had the main switch connected to the meter been damaged. Therefore, there was no possibility of a short circuit, he said.

Will be doubtful of probe’s impartiality after home minister’s remarks: Nusrat Tabassum

Speaking in parliament on Thursday, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said he believed no petrol bomb had been used at the site. 

Given the age of the electrical wiring, the possibility of an electrical short circuit was very high, he said. 

However, he added that if a more thorough investigation established evidence of sabotage, the government would take appropriate action.

I will keep doing my work walking through fire: Nusrat Tabassum

Meanwhile, a committee formed by the Ministry of Home Affairs has begun investigating the fire at Nusrat’s ancestral home. At around 10.30 am today, committee members visited the house in Bagoan village of Daulatpur upazila. They questioned Shah Alam, a resident of the house, and Nusrat’s father, Abdul Halim, about various details of the incident and what had happened at the time.

However, in a post on her Facebook account around midnight on Thursday, Nusrat Tabassum said that, following the home minister’s remarks in parliament regarding the alleged petrol bomb attack on her village home in Kushtia, she would remain sceptical about the impartiality of the investigation.

The fire broke out late on Wednesday night at Nusrat’s ancestral home in Bagoan village of Daulatpur, Kushtia.

Nusrat’s home fire: Heated exchanges in parliament over cause of blaze

She filed a case with Daulatpur police station, alleging that her family members had been targeted in an attempted murder through arson and an explosion at the house. 

The case names leaders of the banned Bangladesh Chhatra League, as well as the Awami League’s affiliated organisations, the Jubo League and Swechchhasebak League, whose activities have been banned in the country, from Kushtia district and Daulatpur upazila.

item.title: Bollywood bolsters security as underworld fears return
item.description:
INDIA-ENTERTAINMENT-CINEMA-BOLLYWOOD

It sounds like a Bollywood thriller, but a spate of shootings and extortion threats targeting Mumbai's stars has sent the industry scrambling for bodyguards, reviving memories of the underworld's grip on cinema in the 1990s.

From gunshots to cash demands, the incidents have unsettled the Indian industry, decades after police crackdowns weakened the criminal gangs once deeply embedded in the multi-billion-dollar business.

Police have linked the latest violence to the gang of Lawrence Bishnoi, a convicted Indian gangster accused by US prosecutors of directing a global criminal network from behind bars.

"Stars are moving around with bodyguards on either side," actor and security agency owner Ronit Roy said.

"There has been a sharp increase in demand... Requests have expanded beyond just lead actors, to include family members and children."

Author S Hussain Zaidi, a former investigative journalist, said opportunistic criminals were exploiting the notoriety of established gangsters.

"Some desperadoes are opening fire in the air to scare the industry and spread fear," Zaidi told AFP.

Now so many guns around me: Salman Khan opens up on receiving death threat

"And they have succeeded -- as people have started believing that the mafia-dominated 1990s era is back."

The latest incidents include gunfire targeting actor Tiger Shroff's car in Mumbai in October, and an alleged $600,000 extortion demand against actor Tusshar Kapoor.

Police have arrested 13 people under organised crime laws in connection with the October shooting, alleging it was intended to extort money, establish gang dominance and spread fear.

Police said there had also been surveillance of other prominent figures.

They have named Anil Pandit, an alleged Bishnoi gang member, as wanted in connection with the shooting.

Darkest periods

Anxiety reverberating across the industry has spilt into public view.

Bollywood superstar Amitabh Bachchan recently greeted fans from behind a bulletproof enclosure outside his Mumbai home during his customary Sunday appearance, while security was beefed up around actor Shah Rukh Khan's home for his birthday.

But Zaidi said the major gangsters of the 1990s were now dead, imprisoned or inactive.

"The only gangster we hear of these days is Lawrence Bishnoi and even he is in jail, so there is no way that any local Mumbai-based gangster has control over the city," he said.

Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff shot at in Mumbai, three suspects held: police

The late 1990s and early 2000s were among Bollywood's darkest periods, when criminal syndicates used threats, extortion and violence to influence film financing, casting and distribution.

They included Dawood Ibrahim, a UN-sanctioned fugitive accused of involvement in the 1993 Mumbai bombings that killed 257 people, and his former lieutenant turned rival Chhota Rajan, who is behind bars in India.

Producers were pressured to pay protection money, surrender business interests and bow to gangsters' demands.

The underworld's influence waned as police intensified operations, strengthened by laws passed in 1999 targeting organised crime, while the growth of corporate financing further reduced gangsters' influence over the film business.

'We will kill you'

Rajiv Rai, director of the hit thriller "Gupt", received extortion demands and threatening calls in the late 1990s before eventually leaving India for Britain.

"I was the victim in the 1990s, the world knows," he told AFP.

Watching the latest incidents unfold, Rai said the motives were harder to decipher.

Bishnoi's gang has been linked to threats against Salman Khan, reportedly over allegations that the Bollywood star had hunted blackbuck antelopes in 1998.

Amitabh Bachchan’s bungalow targeted in threat email, Police launch probe

The animals are revered by the Bishnoi community, a Hindu sect whose faith places strong emphasis on wildlife protection.

Indian authorities have also accused gang members of opening fire outside Khan's Mumbai home and of involvement in the killing of Baba Siddique, a prominent politician with close ties to the film industry, in 2024.

After the October shooting targeting Shroff, a social media post and audio message attributed to a Bishnoi gang associate reportedly claimed responsibility, citing the actor's closeness to Khan.

"In the 1990s, we knew their agenda... ransom money," Rai said.

"Now they are calling and saying if you are Salman's friend, we will kill you... now what kind of agenda is this?"

Ahmed Ali, a crime journalist, said he believed that "many of these seem to be prank calls, to cash in on the situation that Bishnoi has created".

Producer Boney Kapoor, who was targeted by underworld figures over a dispute involving overseas distribution rights for his 1997 Salman Khan film "Judwaa", believes the latest wave of violence will be "short-lived".

"I don't feel that kind of fear," he said. "But one has to be cautious, these shootings can't be ignored."

item.title: Multi-vehicle collision leaves MP, 50 others injured in Gopalganj
item.description:
At least 51 people, including Gopalganj-1 MP Salimuzzaman Salim, were injured in a multi-vehicle collision involving around 20 vehicles in Gopalganj on Friday.
The accident occurred in the Boraitala area of the Dhaka-Barisal highway in the morning.
According to eyewitnesses and police, the MP was on his way to attend a protest meeting in Boraitala when a passenger bus operated by Dolphin Paribahan slammed into the rear of a truck carrying paddy.
The impact caused the truck to lose control and hit vehicles ahead, triggering a chain collision involving 15 to 20 vehicles.
The rear of the private car carrying the MP was badly crushed. Several other vehicles in his convoy, along with passenger buses, easybikes and motorcycles, were also damaged.
Rescuers took the injured to Muksudpur Upazila Health Complex and nearby clinics, where they received treatment.
Traffic on the Dhaka-Barisal highway remained suspended for nearly an hour following the accident.
Later, Bhanga Highway Police removed the damaged vehicles from the road, allowing traffic to return to normal.

item.title: Tk32,000 minimum wage: Owners consider shutting 210 factories
item.description:
Bangladesh’s garment industry is facing growing uncertainty as workers continue demanding higher wages, while factory owners consider shutting down operations over production disruptions, vandalism and security concerns.
Owners of 210 garment factories in Ashulia, Jamgora and Hemayetpur are considering an indefinite closure following continued labour unrest. A preliminary decision was taken at an emergency meeting on Wednesday, with a final decision expected at a meeting of all members on Saturday, Sparrow Group Managing Director Shovon Islam said.
Industry sources said production was suspended at 143 factories in the three areas on Wednesday. In many factories, workers reported for duty but refused to work, while some punched their attendance cards and left. Several factories also reported vandalism, with production remaining suspended at some units for up to 11 consecutive days.
Seven factories in Savar and Ashulia have already been declared closed indefinitely under Section 13(1) of the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006. They include three units of Arunima Group, three of Newage Group and one of Jeans Manufacturing Company Ltd.
Meanwhile, protests over wage demands continued on Thursday. Workers from several factories blocked the Dhaka-Tangail highway in the Mouchak area of Kaliakair, Gazipur, triggering long traffic queues. Police and Border Guard Bangladesh personnel used sound grenades to disperse the protesters. Owners subsequently declared holidays at eight to nine factories in and around Mouchak.
Industrial Police-1 Superintendent Mohammad Mominul Islam Bhuiyan said most factories in Ashulia operated on Thursday, although workers at some units left after marking attendance. Law enforcers continued patrols and surveillance.
The unrest comes as the newly formed minimum wage board considers workers’ demands. At its second meeting, the workers’ representative proposed a monthly minimum wage of Tk32,000. The employers’ representative is expected to present a counterproposal at the board’s third meeting on Monday.
Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) President Mahmud Hasan Khan said wage discussions could not continue alongside disorder. He said the owners were willing to resolve the issue through talks but stressed the need to ensure normal production and discipline.
The disruptions are affecting both workers and businesses. Workers risk losing wages and working days, while owners continue to bear factory rent, utility bills, loan instalments and other operating costs even when production stops.
There are also concerns that delayed shipments could prompt international buyers to seek discounts, cancel orders or shift future business to other countries.
Sparrow Group Managing Director Shovon Islam said shifting production to subcontracting factories would not necessarily solve the problem, as buyers often impose specific requirements on factories, production processes and quality control. Delayed shipments could also force exporters to use costly air freight or risk losing orders.
Former BGMEA director and Bangladesh Apparel Voice CEO Mahiuddin Rubel said both workers and businesses suffer from such disruptions, while instability could damage Bangladesh’s reputation as a sourcing destination.
CPD Distinguished Fellow Dr Fahmida Khatun called for regular dialogue, transparent wage-setting and effective grievance mechanisms. She said fair wages and safe working conditions must be balanced with the industry's production costs and international competitiveness, while buyers should also ensure fair prices for garments.

item.title: Dhaka-Chittagong highway: 13km tailback leaves commuters stranded
item.description:
A 13km traffic jam on the Comilla-bound lane of the Dhaka-Chittagong highway caused severe suffering for passengers and drivers on Friday, leaving long-distance buses, trucks and other vehicles stranded for hours.
The congestion began around 7:30am after a covered van broke down on the approach to the Meghna-Gomti Bridge in Daudkandi, disrupting traffic towards Comilla. As the number of vehicles grew, the tailback stretched nearly 13km through the Gazaria section.
Vehicles were moving slowly or stopping intermittently at several points along the highway, according to local residents and police.
Shahabuddin, a bus passenger travelling to his village home, said he regularly faced delays while travelling between Dhaka and his hometown, particularly on holidays and during family occasions. He questioned when a lasting solution to the recurring congestion would come.
Truck driver Sirajul Islam Pintu said it took him one and a half hours to reach Bhaterchar bus stand after getting stuck in traffic near Jamaldi.
Another truck driver, Shakil Mia, said he spent around an hour travelling from Jamaldi to Anarpura bus stand.
Moniruzzaman, in-charge of the Bhaberchar Highway Police Outpost, said the breakdown of the covered van near the bridge had caused the congestion.
Authorities were working to remove the vehicle, and traffic could return to normal within an hour, he said.
Passengers and transport workers have long faced delays on different stretches of the highway, with commuters calling for quicker removal of broken-down vehicles and measures to ensure smoother traffic movement.

item.title: Mongla Port capacity set to expand with rising domestic, foreign investment
item.description:
The government's renewed focus on Mongla Sea Port is attracting more domestic and foreign investment, raising expectations that the country's second-largest seaport will become a major economic hub in the southwestern region.
The growing investment is expected to boost the port's handling capacity, create substantial employment opportunities and accelerate industrialization and trade across Khulna, Bagerhat, Satkhira and Jessore districts.
Port authorities said ongoing infrastructure development would transform Mongla into a modern seaport.
Since forming the government, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has visited Mongla Port twice, on October 22 and November 5.
During his visit on November 5, he laid the foundation stone for the construction of 2 new jetties at an estimated cost of Tk4,068.23 crore.
Of the project cost, Tk3,592.90 crore will come as a loan from China's Exim Bank, while the Bangladesh government will provide Tk475.33 crore.
Once completed by December 2028, the project is expected to increase the port's annual container handling capacity to around 394,000 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs).
Meanwhile, dredging of the Pashur Channel is underway under a Tk1,538.19 crore project. Work began in July 2026 and is scheduled for completion in December 2029.
Upon completion, ships with a draft of 9.5 to 10 meters will be able to berth directly at the Mongla Port jetties, according to port authorities.
To strengthen operational efficiency and security, 2 powerful tugboats are also being procured under an ongoing project. The procurement process is underway for a buoy-laying vessel, a search-and-rescue vessel, a mother vessel, and a hydrographic survey and research vessel.
Besides, the Khulna-Mongla railway line has been constructed under an Indian-funded Line of Credit (LoC) project. A separate project to protect the marine environment by removing waste and spilled oil from ships is nearing completion.
State Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change Shaikh Faridul Islam, MP, said Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's visits to Mongla Port within just 2 weeks of forming the government reflected the special attention being given to the port.
He expressed optimism that the prime minister's visits would encourage further domestic and foreign investment centered on the port, transforming it into an economic hub for the southwestern region.
He said industrialization, expansion of trade and increased foreign investment would create employment opportunities for hundreds of thousands of young people, improve the socioeconomic conditions of the region and accelerate the country's ambition to become a trillion-dollar economy.
Talking to this correspondent, Rear Admiral Arif Ahmed Mustafa, chairman of Mongla Port Authority, said the foundation stone had been laid for a major Tk4,068 crore project to develop the port into a modern economic hub.
Under the project, jetties No 10 and 11, a container yard covering around 227,000 square meters and a container freight station will be constructed.
These facilities will significantly increase container storage capacity and speed up cargo handling, he added.
He also said an initiative had been taken to introduce direct container train services from Kamalapur Inland Container Depot (ICD) in Dhaka to Mongla Port, which would facilitate faster and cheaper transportation of goods.
Speaking at the inauguration ceremony of the Mongla Port Employees' Association on November 6, Shipping Minister Shaikh Rabiul Alam said Mongla Port had created enormous economic and strategic opportunities for the southwestern region and the country as a whole.
He said the government had taken various steps, including modernization and infrastructure development, to establish the port as a major economic hub in the southern region.
Rabiul Alam said the establishment of a China Export Processing Zone (EPZ) and other major industrial enterprises would expand economic activities in Khulna, Bagerhat, Satkhira and Jessore districts.
Expansion of the highway from Bhanga to Mongla and the development of new rail connections were also progressing, creating prospects for substantial investment and employment.
He said improved road, river and rail connectivity would turn Mongla into a regional transit hub.
Located only 188 kilometers from Kolkata, the seaport was also gaining additional commercial advantages over Chittagong Port due to easier road access.
Sources said work was also underway to establish economic zones near the port, including the China-Bangladesh Mongla Port Economic Zone.
The proposed facilities for manufacturing, warehousing and logistics are expected to encourage new industries along the Mongla-Bhanga corridor.
Lauding the government's initiatives and the prime minister's recent visits to Mongla Port, businesspeople expressed satisfaction, saying the port had significant potential once the government's development initiatives, including the new jetty construction project, were completed.
They also expressed concern over persistent operational challenges, particularly the navigability crisis in the Pashur River.
Talking to this correspondent, Mosharraf Hossain, president of the Mongla Port Customs Agents Association, said the country's second-largest seaport was gradually losing its competitive edge because of inadequate navigability in the river in the past.
The Mongla Port Authority (MPA) also earned a profit of over Tk400 crore this year due to immediate dredging initiatives by the present government, he said.
Mosharraf also said large vessels had to unload most of their cargo at the outer anchorage before entering the port, increasing transportation costs and disrupting schedules.
As a result, container traders were increasingly shifting to Chittagong Port because of difficulties in ensuring the timely delivery of goods.
"The government initiatives will increase vessel arrivals," he said, adding that they would resolve the navigability problem permanently.
He also called for a high-level government monitoring team to oversee dredging activities and prevent irregularities in project implementation.
Captain Md Rafiqul Islam, chairman of the Bangladesh Shipping Agents Association, Khulna, said large vessels could not reach the jetties directly and had to unload nearly half of their cargo at the outer anchorage before proceeding to the port with the remaining goods.
Emphasizing the need for a permanent solution, Rafiqul Islam, who has been involved in the shipping business since 1993, said the authorities generally addressed problems as they emerged but rarely focused on their root causes through long-term planning.
He said adopting planned management practices similar to those followed at river ports in developed countries could ensure navigability for the next 10 to 15 years without recurring problems.
Contacted by this correspondent, Zulfikar Ali, general secretary of the Mongla Port Berth and Ship Operators Association, identified 3 major reasons behind the decline in vessel movements: navigability problems, a reduction in container ship arrivals and fewer gas-carrying vessels.
He said fewer than half the container ships that previously called at the port were now arriving because of inadequate navigability.
Higher container transportation costs from Mongla and frequent disruptions to vessel schedules were also discouraging traders.
Zulfikar Ali said exporters often faced difficulties loading goods onto ships within scheduled deadlines, sometimes prompting foreign buyers to refuse shipments. To avoid such risks, many businesses were increasingly opting for Chittagong Port, he added.
Mongla Port users also expressed hope that Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's recent visits to the port would usher in a new era in its history. They added that completion of the new projects would help transform the port into an economic hub for the southwestern and northwestern regions.

item.title: Microsoft services disrupted worldwide as recovery efforts continue
item.description:
Microsoft is continuing efforts to restore its Microsoft 365 services after a global outage disrupted Outlook, Teams, Copilot and other platforms, with some systems showing signs of improvement but service capacity yet to return to normal.
The disruption, which began on Thursday, affected services connected to Microsoft's Exchange Online and email infrastructure, leaving users in several countries unable to access their mailboxes, send or receive emails, view recently used files and access some other Microsoft 365 features.
Microsoft's affected services included Outlook, Microsoft Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft Copilot 365, Microsoft Planner, Microsoft To Do and several administrative, security and education features.
In its latest update on Friday, Microsoft reported incremental improvements across several affected services. However, it said service health remained variable and system capacity had not fully returned to normal levels.
"Recovery actions are ongoing and have progressed in phases across affected Microsoft 365 infrastructure," the company said, adding that it was monitoring system performance and customer reports as it continued its recovery efforts.
Microsoft also said it was prioritizing email queues and backlog processing to protect delayed messages. As part of the recovery measures, it extended the email timeout window to 48 hours to help preserve emails delayed by the disruption.
Earlier, the company reported that a large number of servers had become unexpectedly unavailable, shifting workloads onto the remaining infrastructure. Microsoft said it was working to restore affected servers, improve traffic management and apply technical changes to stabilize its systems.
Although some recovery measures initially showed positive results, Microsoft acknowledged that its earlier adjustments had not consistently restored services. The company said it had no indication that the outage was caused by malicious activity.
The disruption was reported across dozens of countries, with outage-monitoring platform Downdetector recording roughly 130,000 reports of problems accessing Outlook on Thursday. The number of reports subsequently declined.
The outage also affected businesses and government operations in several countries. Singapore's Government Technology Agency reported problems with government email services, while the Philippines' Supreme Court said the disruption had affected some of its operations, including email responses.
In Japan, the government's IT infrastructure was also affected, prompting authorities to arrange alternative communication methods. Some businesses and banking operations in Hong Kong reported disruptions.
Technology companies OpenAI and Anthropic also reported problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools. Meanwhile, Indian airlines IndiGo and Air India experienced disruptions to their email support services, although both companies said their flight operations remained unaffected.
Microsoft says more than 430 million people use its Microsoft 365 applications. The ongoing disruption has highlighted the widespread reliance of businesses, government institutions and individual users on the company's cloud-based services.
The company has said its engineering teams are continuing to monitor affected infrastructure and implement recovery measures until services are fully restored.

item.title: 291,209 students seek HSC answer script re-evaluation
item.description:
A total of 291,209 students have applied for re-scrutiny and re-evaluation of 1,087,413 answer scripts in various subjects under all 11 education boards following the publication of this year's Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) and equivalent examination results.
Among the 11 education boards, the Dhaka Education Board received the highest number of applications for answer script re-scrutiny, followed by the Chittagong Education Board.
According to board-wise statistics, the Dhaka Education Board received the highest number of applications, at 335,879, while the Chittagong Education Board received the second-highest number, totaling 117,700.
Among the other boards, Rajshahi received 109,971 applications, Jessore 97,618, Comilla 92,776, Dinajpur 89,420, Mymensingh 71,762, Barisal 53,409, Sylhet 51,243, Madrasah Education Board 40,830 and Technical Education Board 26,806 applications for re-scrutiny of answer scripts.
Speaking on the issue, President of the Inter-Education Board Coordination Committee and Chairman of the Dhaka Education Board Professor Syed Akhtaruzzaman said the examination and assessment systems had been made fully objective and impartial over the past 2 years.
He said answer scripts had been evaluated according to a prescribed set of standards, and the same method had also been followed last year.
Following the recent publication of HSC results, it was found that students had performed poorly in compulsory subjects such as English, Bangla and Information and Communication Technology (ICT) across all education boards.
He said the failure rate in these subjects was also high. Taking into consideration the comparatively poor results and the high number of failures, the education boards had already started working on the matter.
Identifying the shortage of teachers as a major reason behind the poor results, he said: “Many colleges do not have sufficient ICT teachers. Even in government colleges, teachers from other disciplines are assigned to teach ICT due to the absence of subject-specific teachers.”
Subject-wise statistics of the Dhaka Education Board show that a large number of applications for answer script re-scrutiny have been submitted not only in Bangla, English and ICT but also in important subjects under the Science, Humanities and Business Studies groups.
According to the statistics, an equal number of 42,002 applications were submitted for English First Paper and Second Paper, while 38,075 applications were received for ICT.
These 2 subjects recorded the highest numbers of answer script re-scrutiny applications under the Dhaka Education Board.
An analysis of the statistics shows that, alongside English, a significant number of applications were also submitted for re-scrutiny of Bangla answer scripts among the compulsory subjects.
An equal number of 24,858 applications were submitted for Bangla First Paper and Second Paper.
Among the important Science group subjects, Chemistry received the highest number of applications, with an equal 18,482 applications for both First Paper and Second Paper.
Besides, an equal number of 15,757 applications were submitted for re-scrutiny of Biology answer scripts in both First Paper and Second Paper.
In the Humanities group, an equal 3,571 applications were submitted for Civics and Good Governance First Paper and Second Paper, while 1,997 applications were received for Social Work.
Among the Business Studies group subjects, Accounting received the highest number of applications.
An equal 3,827 applications were submitted for Accounting First Paper and Second Paper.
Besides, 2,331 applications were received for re-scrutiny of Business Organization and Management answer scripts.
The Ministry of Education said the pass rate in the HSC and equivalent examinations, the results of which were published on October 31, stood at 52.12% across the 11 education boards.
Of the total 1,240,798 examinees, 646,685 students passed, while 40,084 secured GPA-5.
Failing to achieve their expected results, 291,209 students under the 11 boards applied for re-scrutiny of 1,087,413 answer scripts.
The deadline for submitting applications was 12 noon on November 8.
Sources at the Ministry of Education and education boards said significant changes had also been observed following the re-scrutiny of this year's Secondary School Certificate (SSC) and equivalent examination results.
Of the total 1,829,485 examinees under the 11 education boards in the SSC and equivalent examinations, 402,052 students applied for re-evaluation of their results, involving a total of 1,287,926 answer scripts.
Following re-scrutiny, a total of 4,585 students across the country who had initially failed in the SSC examinations passed, while another 3,079 students secured GPA-5.
The Inter-Education Board authorities said strict disciplinary action would also be taken against the concerned examiners and chief examiners if major inconsistencies in answer script assessment or significant discrepancies in marks were found during the HSC re-evaluation, as had happened in the SSC examinations.
President of the Inter-Education Board Coordination Committee Professor Syed Akhtaruzzaman said more than 100 examiners and chief examiners had been identified for major deviations in answer script assessment during the SSC examinations.
He said specific diagnostic assessments were being conducted on their cases, and recommendations for disciplinary action were being sent to the Ministry of Education.
If similar cases of unjustified marking or excessive differences in marks were found during the HSC result re-scrutiny, recommendations would be made for disciplinary action against the examiners and chief examiners responsible for negligence in assessing answer scripts, following the same procedure.
He made it clear that inappropriate or faulty assessment would primarily be determined by examining the difference between the marks obtained by a student before and after re-scrutiny. Necessary action would be taken accordingly.
According to the action plan of the Inter-Education Board, after receiving students' applications for re-scrutiny of HSC and equivalent examination results through the website, the application data will be collected from the Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET).
Subsequently, the Computer Cell will send lists containing answer script information and subject-wise details to the relevant sections. Examiners will be appointed for re-evaluation, and answer scripts will be collected from the chief examiners.
In the next phase, re-evaluation work will begin following a briefing for the appointed examiners.
It was further stated that after completing the assessment, the statements signed by the re-evaluation examiners, along with the answer scripts whose marks have been changed, will be sent to the Computer Cell.
The Computer Cell will then enter the revised marks and verify the litho codes of the answer scripts. Following the final verification of the revised answer scripts, the results of the re-scrutiny and re-evaluation will be published.
The Dhaka Education Board said the re-scrutiny process for this year's HSC examination answer scripts had begun.
The process started on November 11 with the participation of examiners and concerned officials.
It will continue until November 17, from 9am to 5pm every day, at the Higher Secondary Examination Section on the seventh and eighth floors of Building No 4 of the board.
Senior System Analyst of the Dhaka Education Board Engineer Md Monjurul Kabir said the processing of hundreds of thousands of online applications and related data submitted for HSC answer script re-scrutiny would be carried out with utmost caution.
He said the board's ICT team was closely monitoring the entire process to ensure that no inconsistencies occurred in the changes to marks following publication of the results.

item.title: High vegetable, fish and meat prices keep Dhaka consumers under pressure
item.description:
Winter has yet to fully set in in Dhaka, but consumers are already facing high prices for vegetables and other essential food items, with little relief in the markets for fish, meat and eggs.
Vegetable prices usually begin to fall as winter approaches and supplies of seasonal produce increase. However, the expected decline is yet to materialise, leaving consumers struggling to manage their daily expenses.
The situation was observed during visits to several kitchen markets in the capital on Friday.
Vendors said supplies of winter vegetables remained limited as the season had not fully begun. Prices may ease in the coming weeks as more seasonal produce reaches the markets.
A market survey found that new potatoes were selling at Tk140-160 per kg, while old potatoes cost Tk30. Green chillies were priced at Tk120 per kg, round eggplants at Tk100, long eggplants at Tk60-80, bitter gourds at Tk80-100, beans at Tk80-120 depending on variety, cucumbers at Tk100 and carrots at Tk100.
Cauliflowers were selling at Tk50-80 per kg, depending on size. Ridge gourds, pointed gourds, snake gourds, okra and radishes were priced at Tk60 per kg.
Fish prices also remained largely unchanged, with most varieties selling at elevated rates.
Rohu was selling at Tk280-380 per kg, large tilapia at Tk180-200, silver carp and grass carp at Tk180-200, and pangas at Tk160-250.
Katla was priced at Tk350-380 per kg, farmed koi at Tk200-220 and pabda at Tk380-420.
Ilish remained beyond the reach of many consumers, selling at Tk800-2,300 per kg, while larger fish cost more than Tk2,600 per kg.
A dozen brown eggs were selling at Tk145-150, while white eggs cost Tk130-135, adding to consumers' daily expenses.
Meat prices also remained largely unchanged from the previous week. Broiler chicken was selling at Tk170-190 per kg and Sonali chicken at Tk240-330.
Beef was priced at Tk800-850 per kg, while mutton cost Tk1,200-1,250.
Sijan Rahman, a vegetable seller at Dhupkhola market, said supplies of fresh winter vegetables were still limited.
"Prices will fall once new vegetables start arriving in the markets. They may come down somewhat after another week. When several varieties of the same vegetable become available, it is a sign that prices are starting to fall," he said.
Sheikh Nayeem, who was shopping at Sutrapur market, said high prices had made it difficult for ordinary consumers to buy vegetables and fish.
"I cannot afford to buy many vegetables because of their high prices. It will become difficult to run a household if things continue like this," he said.
He added that he eventually left the fish market without buying anything because of the high prices.
"Fish that used to cost Tk800 now cannot be found even for Tk1,200. If the prices of essential commodities continue to rise like this, it will become increasingly difficult for ordinary people to manage their households," he said.

item.title: Sri Lanka: Rights groups sound alarm over proposed anti-terror law
item.description:
For 46-year-old Ganesan (name changed) from Batticaloa in eastern Sri Lanka, any discussion of terrorism brings back memories of his two-year-old daughter, who was killed in the 2019 Easter Sunday attacks. She was one of 270 people who lost their lives in a series of coordinated bombings targeting three churches and three luxury hotels across the island nation.
The attacks were the deadliest in Sri Lanka since the end of its civil war in 2009. More than 500 people were injured.
Ganesan’s daughter was killed in an attack on the Zion Church in Batticaloa.
But Ganesan remains skeptical when asked about the new counterterrorism bill pushed by the government in Sri Lanka.
“Laws against terrorism are necessary to prevent terrorist attacks, but they should not target the innocent or suppress human rights,” he told DW.
The administration led by President Anura Kumara Dissanayake and his National People’s Power faction
has proposed the Protection of the State from Terrorism Act (Psta) as a replacement for the existing Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA). The PTA has many critics who claim that the contentious law has enabled arbitrary detention and the torture of detainees for decades.
The government argues that a robust anti-terrorism law is needed to address the increasingly complex local and international activities of extremist groups.
Rights groups are now also sharply criticizing the new bill. Activist argue that the changes will not bring about any improvement, warning that the draft features an overly broad definition of terrorism, provides inadequate judicial oversight, and grants extensive powers to law enforcement authorities. Activists also warn that the proposed law has only limited safeguards against official abuse.
The bill, for instance, allows security forces to stop, search and question individuals on the basis of “reasonable suspicion,” enter and search premises, and seize items on suspicion of them being linked to an offense under the terrorism act.
“The definition of the term ‘terrorism’ in the bill as presently drafted is highly problematic. The term is unclear, and its meaning has not been clearly defined,” Visakesa Chandrasekaram, a film director and human rights lawyer, told DW.
“Such lack of clarity in the law may result in violations of the fundamental rights of the people,” he added.
Chandrasekaram also pointed out that the bill would confer police powers on the military, which is neither trained to investigate criminal offenses nor equipped to protect the rights of people targeted in such investigations.
This, he warned, could lead to the “militarization” of the law enforcement process.
Dhanushka Silva, a lawyer, said the proposed law is not much different from the existing one.
“The present government pledged to repeal the PTA in their 2024 election manifesto. But now the government seems to replace it with a new act that is a replica of the PTA,” he told DW.
Silva believes the new bill, Psta, could be misused to suppress democratic freedoms and muzzle dissent and free speech.
Under Section 9 of the Psta, even posts or statements made on social media could be subject to scrutiny due to the broad definition of terrorism-related offenses in the bill, he explained.
The section further suggests that individuals who share content deemed to be a terrorism offense could face up to 15 years of rigorous imprisonment, according to the lawyer.
“This is a big blow to freedom of speech in a democratic society like ours,” he said.
The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (Ohchr) has also called on the government to ensure that the bill is consistent with international human rights law.
It noted that the Psta, despite containing some additional safeguards and improvements on previous drafts, reproduces a number of shortcomings in the PTA and other, older counter-terrorism bills.
The legislation “should include robust safeguards against torture, ill-treatment, enforced disappearance and coercive interrogation,” Ohchr said in a statement.
Government spokesperson Nalinda Jayatissa, however, rejected the allegations by rights activists and insisted that the new law would not compromise civil liberties and press freedom.
Passing the new counterterrorism legislation could also have economic and foreign policy ramifications for Sri Lanka.
The United Nations, which has repeatedly urged Colombo to repeal the PTA, has called for further revisions to the proposed Psta.
The European Union has likewise urged Sri Lanka to uphold its international human rights obligations if it wishes to continue benefiting from the bloc’s Generalized Scheme of Preferences Plus (GSP+), which grants preferential access to the EU market to eligible developing countries.
Failure to meet these requirements could result in the suspension of GSP+ preferences, likely to trigger significant economic penalties for the country.
During a parliamentary debate on November 12, Speaker Jagath Wickramaratne said that some provisions of the proposed law were inconsistent with the constitution.
The legislation was also challenged before the Supreme Court, which outlined several amendments and said Parliament could pass the measure once the changes were made.
Parliament has yet to set a date for a vote.

item.title: Opposition MPs to visit Nusrat's fire-ravaged Kushtia home
item.description:
An opposition parliamentary team is scheduled to visit the home of reserved-seat MP Nusrat Tabassum in Daulatpur upazila of Kushtia on Friday afternoon, following an alleged arson attack.
The team is scheduled to reach her residence in Baguan village at 3pm, according to Yeasir Arafat, the media secretary of the National Citizen Party (NCP).
After inspecting the fire-damaged house, the team is expected to hold a press briefing.
The team comprises NCP joint conveners and MPs Advocate Abdullah Al Amin and Mahmuda Alam Mitu, Chuadanga-1 MP Md Masud Parves and Kushtia-2 MP Md Abdul Gafur.
Earlier, Nusrat filed an attempted murder case with Daulatpur Police Station on Thursday night in connection with the alleged arson attack.
The case names eight people and 25 to 30 unidentified individuals as accused.
The named accused include the president and general secretary of the Daulatpur upazila unit of the banned Bangladesh Chhatra League, the president and general secretary of the Kushtia district unit of Chhatra League , the president and general secretary of the district Jubo League, and the president and general secretary of the Daulatpur upazila unit of Swechchhasebak League.
Earlier, a fire broke out at the MP's ancestral home in Baguan village of Daulatpur around 1:30am on Thursday.
Five of the tin-shed house's eight rooms were burned in the incident, while two goats also died in the fire.
Nusrat alleged that the attackers set fire to her house after throwing petrol bombs in an attempt to kill her family members.

item.title: Australia's Cummins says Khawaja '100 percent wrong' on 'Sandpapergate'
item.description:
Australia captain Pat Cummins on Friday said Usman Khawaja was "100 percent wrong" in claiming the whole team knew about "Sandpapergate", calling it "complete and utter nonsense".
The retired Khawaja reopened old wounds with the release of his autobiography this week and a chapter dealing with the 2018 ball-tampering scandal in South Africa that rocked world cricket.
In the book, the opener alleged that the whole team, including Cummins, knew about the plot to rough up the ball with sandpaper to make it swing.
The scandal centred around the third Test in Cape Town, but Khawaja also claimed the tactic was used in the second Test at Port Elizabeth.
A Cricket Australia probe concluded only David Warner, Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft were in the know, with all three sent home in disgrace and subsequently banned.
Smith was sacked as captain before Tim Paine took over and subsequently Cummins.
"When he says we all knew, if by that he means we knew sandpaper was going out on the field, he's 100 percent wrong," a candid Cummins said at a press conference.
"I said that consistently for the last eight years. I did not know that was happening.
"But I think Usman actually says things that are far more serious than that. He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball tamper with sandpaper.
"That's complete and utter nonsense."
Cummins and fellow bowlers Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon all denied publicly in a 2021 statement that they were aware of the plan.
Warner has this week strongly backed his close friend Khawaja's new version of events.
But Darren Lehmann, who was head coach at the time, denied any knowledge, as did former batting coach Graeme Hick who also rubbished Khawaja's allegations as "absolutely false".
Starc reiterated this week his stance that "we weren't aware of things being taken on the field".
Lyon and Hazlewood have remained silent, as have Smith and Bancroft.
Cummins accused Khawaja of being "flippant" with the way he dropped his bombshell claims eight years after the fact.
"Usman is a friend, but friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations," he said.
"In his book he's been casual with my life and the lives of many others and I think Australian cricket.
"I think the way that he's presented his story, I think he's done that in a very casual manner. And it affects a lot of people."
In a media blitz this week, Khawaja said he spoke in the dressing room after the Cape Town Test urging the team to take collective responsibility, rather than scapegoating Warner, Smith and Bancroft.
But Cummins said he had no recollection of this.
"I don't remember any conversation around collective responsibility. I don't remember any team meeting where he stood up and said, 'Let's own this as a team'," he said.
Cricket Australia has ruled out reopening their investigation with chairman David Boon on Thursday assuring Cummins that his job was safe, regardless.
Cummins admitted the culture of the team around 2018 had an ugly win-at-all-costs mentality, culminating in the Cape Town furore.
But he said since then it had been "absolutely brilliant".
"I didn't like the way we spoke to umpires, the opposition. I think there was a bit of an arrogance and a bit of an ugliness at times that didn't sit well with me as a young guy," he said.
"And now I'm captain, I have spent a lot of time making sure that that's not the case with this current Aussie team."

item.title: Bollywood bolsters security as underworld fears return
item.description:
It sounds like a Bollywood thriller, but a spate of shootings and extortion threats targeting Mumbai’s stars has sent the industry scrambling for bodyguards, reviving memories of the underworld’s grip on cinema in the 1990s.
From gunshots to cash demands, the incidents have unsettled the Indian industry, decades after police crackdowns weakened the criminal gangs once deeply embedded in the multi-billion-dollar business.
Police have linked the latest violence to the gang of Lawrence Bishnoi, a convicted Indian gangster accused by US prosecutors of directing a global criminal network from behind bars.
“Stars are moving around with bodyguards on either side,” actor and security agency owner Ronit Roy said.
“There has been a sharp increase in demand... Requests have expanded beyond just lead actors, to include family members and children.”
Author S. Hussain Zaidi, a former investigative journalist, said opportunistic criminals were exploiting the notoriety of established gangsters.
“Some desperadoes are opening fire in the air to scare the industry and spread fear,” Zaidi told AFP.
“And they have succeeded -- as people have started believing that the mafia-dominated 1990s era is back.”
The latest incidents include gunfire targeting actor Tiger Shroff’s car in Mumbai in October, and an alleged $600,000 extortion demand against actor Tusshar Kapoor.
Police have arrested 13 people under organized crime laws in connection with the October shooting, alleging it was intended to extort money, establish gang dominance and spread fear.
Police said there had also been surveillance of other prominent figures.
They have named Anil Pandit, an alleged Bishnoi gang member, as wanted in connection with the shooting.
Anxiety reverberating across the industry has spilt into public view.
Bollywood superstar Amitabh Bachchan recently greeted fans from behind a bulletproof enclosure outside his Mumbai home during his customary Sunday appearance, while security was beefed up around actor Shah Rukh Khan’s home for his birthday.
But Zaidi said the major gangsters of the 1990s were now dead, imprisoned or inactive.
“The only gangster we hear of these days is Lawrence Bishnoi and even he is in jail, so there is no way that any local Mumbai-based gangster has control over the city,” he said.
The late 1990s and early 2000s were among Bollywood’s darkest periods, when criminal syndicates used threats, extortion and violence to influence film financing, casting and distribution.
They included Dawood Ibrahim, a UN-sanctioned fugitive accused of involvement in the 1993 Mumbai bombings that killed 257 people, and his former lieutenant turned rival Chhota Rajan, who is behind bars in India.
Producers were pressured to pay protection money, surrender business interests and bow to gangsters’ demands.
The underworld’s influence waned as police intensified operations, strengthened by laws passed in 1999 targeting organized crime, while the growth of corporate financing further reduced gangsters’ influence over the film business.
Rajiv Rai, director of the hit thriller “Gupt,” received extortion demands and threatening calls in the late 1990s before eventually leaving India for Britain.
“I was the victim in the 1990s, the world knows,” he told AFP.
Watching the latest incidents unfold, Rai said the motives were harder to decipher.
Bishnoi’s gang has been linked to threats against Salman Khan, reportedly over allegations that the Bollywood star had hunted blackbuck antelopes in 1998.
The animals are revered by the Bishnoi community, a Hindu sect whose faith places strong emphasis on wildlife protection.
Indian authorities have also accused gang members of opening fire outside Khan’s Mumbai home and of involvement in the killing of Baba Siddique, a prominent politician with close ties to the film industry, in 2024.
After the October shooting targeting Shroff, a social media post and audio message attributed to a Bishnoi gang associate reportedly claimed responsibility, citing the actor’s closeness to Khan.
“In the 1990s, we knew their agenda... ransom money,” Rai said.
“Now they are calling and saying if you are Salman’s friend, we will kill you... now what kind of agenda is this?”
Ahmed Ali, a crime journalist, said he believed that “many of these seem to be prank calls, to cash in on the situation that Bishnoi has created.”
Producer Boney Kapoor, who was targeted by underworld figures over a dispute involving overseas distribution rights for his 1997 Salman Khan film “Judwaa,” believes the latest wave of violence will be “short-lived.”
“I don’t feel that kind of fear,” he said. ”But one has to be cautious, these shootings can’t be ignored.”

item.title: Shama calls for predictable, cost-free financing for gender-responsive climate action
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam has called for predictable, accessible and cost-free financing for gender-responsive climate adaptation and resilience.
She made the call while speaking at an event titled “Policy to Practice: Strengthening Gender-responsive Climate Governance and Finance in Bangladesh” at the Bangladesh Pavilion in the Blue Zone of the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkiye, on Thursday.
The event was jointly organised by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, and UN Women Bangladesh. Shama attended the event as the chief guest.
The event highlighted Bangladesh’s experiences, emerging lessons, and implementation challenges, with particular attention to institutional capacity, inter-ministerial coordination, sectoral mainstreaming, and gender-responsive climate finance.
It also explored how development partners and international financial institutions could help strengthen the enabling environment and mobilise resources for country-led climate priorities.
In her remarks, the state minister emphasised that safety, mobility, and participation must be integrated into climate adaptation planning from the outset rather than treated as afterthoughts.
